item.content:encoded:
For the third time in five such games, lefty-swinging Yankees third baseman Ryan McMahon was out of the lineup against a right-handed starter to open Tuesday’s doubleheader.
In all three instances, righty-swinging José Caballero started at third base instead.
Manager Aaron Boone chalked Tuesday afternoon’s decision up to Tampa Bay Rays starter Nick Martinez having reverse splits — meaning he’s actually tougher against lefties — and said McMahon would start the nightcap against a more traditional righty in Drew Rasmussen.
That would also allow the sure-handed McMahon to play defense on a night Max Fried, who regularly elicits grounders to third base, was starting for the Yankees.
But as McMahon continues to struggle, this is a trend to watch with the MLB postseason rapidly approaching.
“I want to be playing them both and getting them both regular reps,” Boone said before Tuesday’s first game, “so [it was] more just picking what game I wanted to play Caballero.”
Entering Tuesday, McMahon was hitting just .150 with a .402 OPS and no home runs since Sept. 1, when he returned from the injured list for a left thumb sprain.
Overall, he is batting .208 with 10 homers and a .618 OPS.
While his season-long numbers against right-handed pitchers (.639 OPS) are superior to his stats against lefties (.518 OPS), McMahon’s offensive production has been modest either way.
Caballero was already the preferred third-base option against left-handed starters, but now he’s seeing more playing time there against right-handers, too.
A utilityman by trade, Caballero began Tuesday with a .237 average, 10 home runs and a .676 OPS against right-handed pitching.
Caballero’s previous two starts against right-handers came on Sunday against Arizona’s Corbin Burnes, whose splits are fairly even for his career, and last week against Minnesota’s Bailey Ober, who is better against righties than lefties.
That means Caballero isn’t only getting chances against right-handed pitchers with reverse splits.
And while McMahon’s calling card is typically his glove, the advanced metrics have not been favorable to the 31-year-old this season.
McMahon entered Tuesday with -1 Defensive Runs Saved and 1 Outs Above Average — down considerably from his 10 DRS and 7 OAA in 2025.
His numbers at third base this year are comparable to those of Caballero, who began the day with 0 DRS and -1 OAA.
Caballero is also much more dynamic on the bases, as he began the doubleheader with 32 stolen bases. However, starting Caballero eliminates the ability to use him as a pinch-runner — an element of his game that makes him a valuable late-inning weapon come October.
Third base isn’t the Yankees’ only infield position with some uncertainty.
Since being replaced at shortstop by George Lombard Jr. and recalled from Triple-A, Anthony Volpe has performed admirably as the Yankees’ second baseman.
The righty-hitting Volpe began Tuesday hitting .286 with a .753 OPS since being recalled on Sept. 10. He had been worth 1 DRS and 1 OAA at second base over that small sample, too.
Volpe is not going to supplant second baseman Jazz Chisholm Jr., who was set to be activated for the second game of the doubleheader after a short IL stint for a right thumb sprain.
But Volpe could challenge for playing time at second base against left-handed pitching, against whom he is hitting .240 with a .680 OPS in the majors this season.
The lefty-swinging Chisholm has endured a down season against lefties, batting .221 with a .654 OPS and a team-worst 35% strikeout rate in those matchups.
“Obviously, Anthony’s done a good job,” Boone said, “but looking forward to getting Jazz back as well.”
The 28-year-old Chisholm wasn’t thrilled last year when the Yankees sat him against left-handed Boston Red Sox ace Garrett Crochet in Game 1 of their Wild Card series.
But with the Yankees likely to face the lefty-heavy Red Sox in the Wild Card round again next week, Boone and company will have more decisions to make at second and third — especially because offense would be at a premium if Aaron Judge (calf) can’t return in time.

item.content:encoded:
Yankees utility player Jose Caballero will get the start today at third base in the first game of a doubleheader at Yankee Stadium against the Tampa Bay Rays.
Caballero (age 30) is a former Tampa Bay Ray who was traded to the Yankees at last year’s MLB trade deadline. Caballero is hitting a .236 batting average with 14 home runs, 51 RBIs, 32 stolen bases, and a .665 OPS.
Ryan McMahon Yankees Dilemma
This is an interesting development, considering third baseman and left-handed hitter Ryan McMahon has been struggling significantly lately, both offensively and defensively.
This season, McMahon is hitting .208 with 10 home runs, 35 RBIs, and a .618 OPS. McMahon’s throws from third base this year have been concerning at times as well. Caballero is an above-average defender and could provide more value offensively than McMahon is right now, so it makes sense why the Yankees are trying Caballero at third base in game one of the doubleheader today against Tampa.
Yankees Getting Ready For Playoffs
With the playoffs (Wild Card) just a week away, with game one beginning Tuesday, September 29th, now is the time for the Yankees to not only rest some key players but also try guys at different positions as they figure out how the postseason roster will ultimately shake out.
The Yankees are also still waiting on the return of Jazz Chisholm Jr., which raises another question: what do the Yankees do when it comes to playing either Anthony Volpe or Jazz Chisholm Jr. at second base, and what happens to the other?
Caballero has talked about trying to provide extra spark/energy to prove himself when playing for his former squad in Tampa. The Yankees will hope to see that effect from a different position in game one of the doubleheader and in this series as they look to wrap up the regular season on a positive note. In contrast, Tampa is looking for a win to clinch the AL East Division, with the winner in a likely wild-card race between the Yankees and Red Sox then going on to face Tampa Bay.
But how Caballero fares today at third base could offer a glimpse into the Yankees’ postseason strategy as they prepare for the Wild Card round, which will be no easy task after navigating the AL East. It will also be interesting to see how much this move affects Ryan McMahon’s playing time for the rest of the regular season and then the postseason, unless they view it as rest for McMahon.

BRONX, NY — Jazz Chisholm Jr. is set to be activated from the 10-day injured list following the first game of the Yankees’ doubleheader on Tuesday against the Tampa Bay Rays.
The second baseman missed two weeks after spraining his thumb, and his spot was filled in admirably by Anthony Volpe — the cast-off shortstop who has enjoyed a minor renaissance, of sorts. Entering Tuesday’s action, he had hit safely in six of his 10 games since being called back up from Triple-A, adding a home run and seven RBI. Five of them came in his first game back on Sept. 10 against the Colorado Rockies.
Yankees manager Aaron Boone said that Chisholm is “in a good spot” after hitting and throwing over the past several days. How playing time will shake out remains to be seen.
“We’ll see,” Boone said. “Obviously, Anthony’s done a good job, but looking forward to getting Jazz back as well.”
With the opportunity for playing time seemingly available at third base with Jose Caballero, Ryan McMahon, and Amed Rosario in the mix, Boone had said that “we’ll see” when asked about Volpe potentially moving to the hot corner. Volpe said he has yet to have those conversations with team brass.
It has been a down season for Chisholm, who owns a .715 OPS with 19 home runs and 55 RBI. After a 30/30 season last year, he came into the 2026 campaign hoping to make a run at 50/50.
That did not happen, but getting a healthy Chisholm back who could possibly recapture last year’s spark would provide a significant boost for the Yankees, who are facing the very real possibility of being without Aaron Judge for their Wild Card Series against the Boston Red Sox next week.

This four-game tilt against the Rays in the penultimate series of the season had the chance to be a blockbuster showdown to decide the division. However, the Yankees losing two out of three to the Diamondbacks removed a lot of the jeopardy from this series, New York now needing to sweep just to avoid being eliminated from the AL East title race and depending on a very unlikely collapse from Tampa in their final series of the season to keep the divisional door the slightest bit ajar. All the same, this could be a preview of a prospective ALCS showdown, so I expect both teams to come out firing. The first game of today’s doubleheader is a makeup of the rainout from May 23rd.
Carlos Rodón finds himself in the unexpected position of being on the postseason rotation bubble. Cam Schlittler and Max Fried are seemingly locks which would pit Rodón against Gerrit Cole for that final spot if they roll out a three-man rotation. It almost comes down to a style choice at that point — Rodón walks almost three times as many batters as Cole, but surrenders about half as many home runs per nine. He’s a good choice to start a game against the Rays — in six starts against Tampa with the Yankees, Rodón has a 3.69 ERA and 31.3-percent strikeout rate in 31.2 innings. In 15 starts this season, Rodón is 6-3 with a 2.95 ERA (142 ERA+), 3.69 FIP, and 83 strikeouts in 76.1 innings.
The Rays have a maddening habit of transforming other teams’ castoffs into rotation stars. This season’s example is longtime journeyman Nick Martinez, who had pitched as a swingman the previous four years in San Diego and Cincinnati. Martinez owns the lowest walk rate (3.5-percent) of any qualified starter, using deception and precise command to induce soft contact. He’s technically got a six-pitch mix but usually sticks with sinker, changeup, cutter, and four-seamer. In 29 starts, Martinez is 15-4 with a 2.94 ERA (142 ERA+), 3.98 FIP, and 101 strikeouts in 171.1 innings.
This is more or less the Yankees’ go-to lineup for the rest of the regular season with Aaron Judge on the IL. Heliot Ramos and Spencer Jones are both going to get a lot of run out in the outfield, so it was encouraging to see them both hit home runs against the former Cy Young winner Corbin Burnes in their last game. José Caballero gets the start over Ryan McMahon at third and sounded eager to make an impact against the team that traded him to the Yankees at last year’s deadline.
The Rays have their three-headed slugging monster atop lineup and then stack the bottom two-thirds with speed. Junior Caminero is third in MLB with 41 home runs giving him back-to-back 40-HR seasons. Chandler Simpson is MLB’s stolen base leader with 46 and third in batting average at .309, but is the only qualified hitter in baseball without a home run this season.

item.content:encoded:
It was easy for everybody to get ahead of themselves when Anthony Volpe had a big first game back against the Colorado Rockies. Jazz Chisholm Jr. had just gone down, and Volpe delivered a three-hit night capped by a grand slam. At that point, Volpe had gone through a torrid home run streak in the minors, so the thought was that if he replicated it in the big leagues, maybe he could usurp Chisholm.
While Volpe's teammates at Triple-A saw the version of him that closely resembled an infield Barry Bonds, he just wasn't that after that first game. Since then, Volpe has gone 7-for-33. He didn't hit a home run and had just two doubles in that span. In many ways, his .226/.263/.290 slash line is about where he has always been as a big leaguer.
That is why, since Chisholm will be playing in the second game of Tuesday night's doubleheader vs. the Rays, per Chris Kirschner of The Athletic, there's no reason to debate who takes second base. The answer is easily Chisholm. Chisholm hasn't had the best season, but in the postseason, he's more of a threat at the plate and on the basepaths. Chisholm has 19 homers this year with 40 stolen bases. Overall, he's hitting .232/.312/.403 at the plate.
Then, of course, there's the defense. That's why a hitter who's been at or below a 100 wRC+ all year can post a 3.2 WAR, according to FanGraphs. This year, Chisholm also has 12 Outs Above Average at the position, per Baseball Savant.
It does feel like Chisholm is the priority, too, once he's back. According to manager Aaron Boone, when asked about Volpe's status and the possibility of him playing at third base, the focus was on getting Chisholm back.
"We'll see," Boone said of Volpe getting reps at the hot corner, according to the New York Post's Greg Joyce. "First things first, getting Jazz back, and then we'll figure it out as the week unfolds, how I want to play it."
Potential infield configuration against a lefty
If the Yankees face a tough lefty in October and aren't too keen on playing Ryan McMahon, who has a 74 wRC+, and Chisholm, they might have a choice here. They could stick with Chisholm at second and have either Jose Caballero or Anthony Volpe play third base.
They could also have Chisholm go back to third base and have Volpe at second. That way, they keep the better player on the field while also getting a righty at second or third.
With Aaron Judge out, Chisholm could boost the lineup. He's had a tough year, but a big October could make up for some regular-season woes.

After Chisholm got hurt diving into second base Sept. 8, the Yankees called up Anthony Volpe to get some run at the position he had mostly transitioned to at Triple-A, and he made the most of it.
In the 10 games since Volpe was recalled, he has started at second base nine times (José Caballero started the other) and mostly looked sharp, batting .286 with a .753 OPS and four steals.
Whether Volpe has done enough to warrant at-bats once Chisholm returns remains to be seen. Shortly before he was called back up, the natural shortstop had also started to mix in some third base, starting three games there, though Aaron Boone would only offer, “We’ll see,” when asked whether that could be an option for Volpe with Chisholm back.
“First things first, getting Jazz back and then we’ll figure it out as the week unfolds how I want to play it,” Boone said.
The Yankees have not gotten much offensive production from their third basemen this year, especially of late. Since returning from his own thumb sprain Sept. 1, Ryan McMahon has hit just 6-for-40 (.150) with a .402 OPS, with Caballero starting at third over him Sunday against a righty. Amed Rosario has often started at third against lefties, and while he has not hit in line with his career numbers, the Yankees continue to believe he will.
Boone could also platoon Volpe and Chisholm at second base, as the lefty-hitting Chisholm is batting only .221 with a .654 OPS against lefties. But the pending free agent had just been starting to get hot in a disappointing season, hitting .391 with a 1.028 OPS over his last 15 games before getting hurt.
If and where Volpe fits on the playoff roster is just one of the many decisions they will have to consider over this final week of the regular season.
“You know it’s going to take a lot of players and a lot of people when you get to spring training and the season unfolds,” Boone said. “We’ll have hopefully some tough decisions to make when we’re setting postseason rosters and things like that. But that’s a better problem to have.”

Clarke Schmidt was expected to see the team doctor early this week after experiencing biceps cramping while warming up Sunday, which kept him from entering the game. The right-hander had just made his return from Tommy John surgery and is trying to carve out a role in the playoff bullpen.
Ryan Weathers (left forearm flexor strain) could also have a role in a playoff bullpen, but first the lefty will need to face hitters this week as he tries to show the Yankees he could jump right into postseason action without pitching in a game since he got hurt Aug. 22.

With Jazz Chisholm Jr. potentially coming off the injured list on Tuesday, former Yankees manager Joe Girardi is suggesting a position change heading into the postseason.
Anthony Volpe now seems entrenched at second base, but Girardi, the last man to lead the Yankees to a World Series in 2009, thinks there's another position for which Chisholm, who has been out with a right thumb sprain, would be suited.
Asked by reporters if he would move Volpe over to third base with the playoffs approaching, manager Aaron Boone said, "We'll see."
"I would think that you would possibly move Jazz over there [to third base] because Jazz has done it," Girardi said on the YES Network during the Yankees' 8-4 loss Sunday to the Arizona Diamondbacks.
"He swung the bat pretty well over there, too," Girardi added. "It didn't seem to phase the offensive part of his game."
Last season, Chisholm played 29 games at third base with a fielding percentage of .920. This season, he has yet to play a game at third.
A year ago, Chisholm batted .242 with 31 home runs, 80 RBIs, 31 stolen bases and an .813 OPS.

item.content:encoded:
PHOENIX -- Varias latas de cerveza fueron vaciadas sobre la cabeza de Aaron Judge mientras el capitán de los Yankees permanecía en el centro del clubhouse de visitantes en el Target Field la semana pasada, rodeado de compañeros eufóricos que celebraban la clasificación del club a la postemporada.
Judge entrecerró los ojos por el ardor y les advirtió a sus compañeros: “Me las van a pagar”.
Aun así, no pretenden que ésa sea su última celebración, pues tienen un firme control del primer puesto del Comodín de la Liga Americana y el título del Este de la Liga Americana todavía está en juego.
“Siempre es bueno cuando puedes celebrar esos momentos durante una temporada”, dijo el manager de los Yankees, Aaron Boone. “Mucha gente dedica mucho tiempo, esfuerzo y sudor. Obviamente, éste es apenas el primer paso de lo que esperamos sean muchos”.
Ahora que aseguraron su pase a la postemporada, ¿qué más les espera a los Yankees?
¿Cómo podría quedar el roster para la postemporada?
C: Austin Wells, Ali Sánchez 
1B: Luis García Jr., Paul Goldschmidt
2B: Jazz Chisholm Jr.
3B: Ryan McMahon, Amed Rosario
SS: George Lombard Jr., José Caballero
OF: Cody Bellinger, Trent Grisham, Spencer Jones, Heliot Ramos
BD: Ben Rice
LA: Gerrit Cole, Cam Schlittler, Max Fried
R: David Bednar, Paul Blackburn, Brent Headrick, Tim Hill, Clarke Schmidt, Michael Fulmer, John Schreiber, Will Warren, Carlos Rodón
Los Yankees utilizaron a 12 lanzadores y a 14 bateadores cuando recibieron a los Medias Rojas en la Serie del Comodín de la Liga Americana del año pasado, así que partiremos de esa misma premisa para el 2026.
Cole está programado para lanzar el miércoles contra Tampa Bay, mientras que Schlittler lo hará el jueves. Mirando hacia adelante, eso sugiere que Cole tendría un día adicional de descanso antes del Juego 1 de la Serie del Comodín de la Liga Americana, mientras que Schlittler estaría con su descanso normal.
Es posible que los Yankees estén alineando a Cole para abrir el Juego 1 y a Schlittler para el Juego 2. Hasta ahora, han preferido no decir mucho al respecto, salvo por la confirmación de Boone de que Cole realizará una apertura en la Serie del Comodín de la Liga Americana.
Rodón podría estar en el bullpen para la serie. En nuestra proyección del roster lo tenemos activo, mientras que el dominicano Luis Gil y Ryan Yarbrough figuran entre quienes quedarían fuera. Ryan Weathers trabaja para regresar como relevista, pero el tiempo juega en su contra. Si está saludable, podría ocupar el lugar de Fulmer o Schreiber.
Chisholm espera regresar esta semana para la serie contra los Rays tras sufrir un esguince en el pulgar derecho, mientras que Grisham ha mostrado mejoría y podría quedarse con un puesto en los jardines. De no ser así, Max Schuemann está entre las alternativas. Otro aspecto para seguir: ¿Podrían los Yankees incluir a Anthony Volpe en lugar de Rosario? Es una posibilidad que vale la pena considerar.
¿Cuándo comenzará la postemporada?
Si los Yankees terminan disputando la Serie del Comodín de la Liga Americana, ésta empezará el 29 de septiembre. La Serie Divisional de la Liga Americana arrancará el 3 de octubre.
¿Contra quién jugarían los Yankees si la temporada terminara hoy?
En estos momentos, sería una revancha de la Serie del Comodín de la Liga Americana del año pasado, con los Yankees recibiendo a los Medias Rojas en el Bronx. Los Yankees ganaron aquella serie dos victorias por una.
Este año, los Yankees tuvieron marca de 7-6 contra Boston.
¿Todavía pueden ganar el Este de la Liga Americana?
Sí, pero tienen un camino cuesta arriba. Los Yankees tienen por delante cuatro enfrentamientos directos con los Rays a partir del martes en el Yankee Stadium, incluyendo una doble-cartelera para abrir la serie. Tampa Bay domina actualmente la serie particular por 6-3, lo que significa que los Yankees necesitarían barrer para quedarse con el criterio de desempate entre ambos.
¿Quién abriría el Juego 1 por los Yankees?
Como se mencionó anteriormente, Cole está programado para lanzar el miércoles frente a Tampa Bay y Schlittler lo hará al día siguiente. Por lo tanto, Cole tendría un día adicional de descanso antes del Juego 1 de la Serie del Comodín de la Liga Americana, mientras que Schlittler estaría con su descanso normal.
Después de permitir siete jonrones en sus dos aperturas anteriores, Cole mermó las dudas externas sobre una posible apertura en los playoffs con una sólida actuación en Arizona. Fried y Rodón han lidiado con lesiones, pero están recuperando su mejor nivel en el momento indicado.
Warren realizará una apertura más durante la serie contra los Orioles, según Boone, pero llegará a los playoffs como una interesante alternativa para el relevo.
¿Será Judge un factor en los playoffs?
Los Yankees han sido poco específicos sobre el estado de Judge. Boone ha evitado ofrecer un plazo estimado para su recuperación e incluso revelar el grado del tirón en la pantorrilla derecha. En términos generales, hasta un tirón de Grado 1, el de menor gravedad, requiere de dos a tres semanas para una recuperación completa.
Es casi seguro que Judge intentará regresar antes. La primera fecha en la que podría ser activado sería para el Juego 162, el 27 de septiembre. Tal como está el panorama ahora mismo, existe una posibilidad muy real de que los Yankees no cuenten con Judge al menos para una potencial Serie del Comodín de la Liga Americana.
Judge dijo que le “gustaría” estar activo para la postemporada y que ése es “el plan”, pero no dijo necesariamente que sería para el 29 de septiembre.
¿Cuáles son las otras preocupaciones en cuanto a lesiones?
Grisham ha avanzado en su programa progresivo de correr y debe de estar disponible para el roster de los playoffs, aunque Boone dijo que no será activado antes de que termine la temporada regular. Chisholm ha estado bateando y realizando tiros, y debe de ser activado durante la serie contra los Rays. Si sufre algún contratiempo, Volpe entraría en consideración.
Y aunque los Yankees no han descartado a Giancarlo Stanton, quien ha estado bateando, han ofrecido pocas novedades sobre su recuperación del más reciente tirón en la pantorrilla.

Why Aaron Boone could be in postseason 'hell' with Yankees originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
The New York Yankees are looking to end a 17-year World Series drought.
Aaron Boone has completed eight of those years as Yankees manager.
This could be a crucial postseason for Boone's future with the AL East club, but New York's ownership and front office have always shown confidence in the skipper.
If three-time MVP Aaron Judge is unable to play in the postseason due to his calf strain, the Yankees will face a difficult task to end their World Series-less streak.
Elsewhere on the diamond, Bleacher Report's Kerry Miller believes Boone will have to hit the right buttons with the infield alignment.
"However, Aaron Boone is about to be in second-guessing hell in October as it pertains to when and where to deploy George Lombard Jr., Anthony Volpe, José Caballero, Amed Rosario and Ryan McMahon at shortstop and third base," Miller wrote.
Second baseman Jazz Chisholm Jr. would complicate things further if he returns from the injured list before the playoffs.
Volpe has been playing well at second base, but Chisholm offers a higher offensive ceiling.
Boone could consider moving Volpe or Chisholm to third base to keep both players in the lineup. If so, does Caballero become limited to pinch-running duties?
McMahon is Boone's best defensive third baseman, but he offers little (.208/.275/.343, .618 OPS) with a bat in hand.
It seems likely Lombard will stick at shortstop, but Boone and his coaching staff have to be racking his brain trying to figure out what's best for the team.

item.content:encoded:
Shortly after getting walked-off by the Diamondbacks on Saturday night, the Yankees acknowledged their reality.
“Mathematically, [it’s] probably pretty tough, but you never know,” Cody Bellinger said of winning the American League East.
Unable to bounce back with an 8-4 loss in Sunday’s series finale against Arizona, the second-place Yankees are now six games back of the division-leading Rays with seven games left in the regular season. The rivals will play four of those games against each other at Yankee Stadium this week, starting with a doubleheader on Tuesday.
Aaron Boone acknowledged that his team will probably have to sweep the Rays just for a crack at the division crown, as FanGraphs gave the Yankees a measly 2.7% chance of winning the AL East before Sunday’s game.
“There’s still a chance,” Cam Schlittler said, “but we gotta play our asses off a little bit.”
While the Yankees still technically have a shot to defy the odds, the far likelier scenario is that their postseason begins on Sept. 29 at home against Boston in the Wild Card round for the second straight year.
With that in mind, let’s try to predict what the club’s roster could look like for that series.
Hitters (15): Ben Rice, Heliot Ramos, Spencer Jones, Trent Grisham, Cody Bellinger, Ryan McMahon, George Lombard Jr., Paul Goldschmidt, Luis García Jr., Jazz Chisholm Jr., José Caballero, Austin Wells, Ali Sánchez, Anthony Volpe, Amed Rosario
With the Yankees providing minimal info on Aaron Judge’s calf strain, it can’t be assumed he’ll be available.
Jazz Chisholm Jr. could return from a sprained thumb as soon as Tuesday. Meanwhile, Trent Grisham is still in play as a playoff option as he recovers from a hamstring strain, but Boone said that activating him before the end of the regular season is “complicated,” partly due to roster logistics.
With Max Schuemann presumably the corresponding move for Chisholm, the Yankees would have to option someone else if they activated Grisham before the playoffs. That someone wouldn’t be able to be recalled for 10 days barring a new injury; it seems like Jasson Domínguez is being protected from that window in case he’s needed for the Wild Card roster.
Grisham has been doing baseball activities and is “pretty deep into his running progression,” Boone said. If he is on the Wild Card roster, the Yankees will have an interesting decision to make between him and Spencer Jones in center field.
Third base could also be a conundrum, as Ryan McMahon and José Caballero don’t offer much offensively, and Amed Rosario is a poor defender. He’s only on the roster as an option against lefties, even though he hasn’t been great against them.
Another idea would be to use Volpe, who has been playing second, at third against lefties since he played a few games there in the minors this season. However, he doesn’t have a strong arm, and he hasn’t been working at third base since being recalled. Volpe said that the Yankees have not talked to him about manning the hot corner before the regular season ends.
“We’ll see,” Boone said. “First things first, getting Jazz back, and then we’ll figure out as the week unfolds how I want to play it.”
Volpe can also play second over Chisholm against lefties.
Pitchers (11): Cam Schlittler, Gerrit Cole, Max Fried, Will Warren, David Bednar, Brent Headrick, Paul Blackburn, Clarke Schmidt, John Schreiber, Tim Hill, Ryan Weathers
As things stand, Carlos Rodón, Max Fried, Gerrit Cole and Cam Schlittler are scheduled to pitch against the Rays, in that order. That would give Cole, who has struggled to get swing-and-miss, an extra day of rest if he were to start Game 1 of the Wild Card round. Schlittler, the AL Cy Young frontrunner, would be on regular rest if tabbed for Game 1.
Because the Wild Card round is a best-of-three series, Rodón isn’t needed, especially with Will Warren expected to work out of the bullpen and able to provide length.
Warren, slated to make one more start this season after struggling on Sunday, is one of a few converted starters who could impact the Bombers’ bullpen this postseason. Clarke Schmidt and Ryan Weathers are the others. Schmidt, being cautious in his return from Tommy John surgery, couldn’t come into Sunday’s game due to some bicep cramping, while Weathers isn’t expected to return from a flexor strain before the regular season ends.
Still, neither Boone nor pitching coach Matt Blake ruled out the idea of Weathers’ first game back coming in the playoffs.
“I don’t know if ‘comfortable’ is [the right word],” Blake said, “but it might be the course of action where he’s the best option even though he hasn’t pitched in the last three or four weeks.”
As for the relievers that the Yankees have leaned on all season, David Bednar, Paul Blackburn and Brent Headrick headline the group. All have been used heavily, especially Headrick.
The lefty allowed a grand slam to Nolan Arenado and saw his fastball velocity down an average of 1.3 mph during his major league-leading 79th appearance on Sunday, but he insisted that he feels fine physically. Boone also downplayed concerns over Headrick’s ongoing velocity fluctuations, though he did say that he hopes to get him and other relievers “in a good spot” with some rest ahead of the playoffs.
That said, the Yankees still haven’t been eliminated from the AL East race. They’ll keep trying to take the division from the Rays until they are.
“We’re going to show up Tuesday,” Boone said, “and try and kick their butt.”

item.content:encoded:
Aaron Judge's regular season may be over, but that doesn't mean the Yankees' has to be.
A mystery calf ailment popped up suddenly on Wednesday and has resulted in the Yankees captain being placed on the injured list. It's unclear whether he will return in 2026, even if he's eligible to return next weekend. Aaron Boone did not give any information on the severity of the calf issue, but the timeline is likely not good due to how tricky those injuries prove to be.
A scenario is now potentially unfolding that would have only appeared in Boone's nightmares: a postseason without the best hitter in baseball, with a lineup that struggled mightily without him. Even if they seemed to gradually improve as time went on, particularly in August, it would be a massive blow if he cannot return.
You can't replace a guy like Judge midseason; you can merely do your best to make up for his absence. Fortunately, on a platoon-heavy team like this, they should have plenty of options to build a lineup without him for the playoffs.
What the playoff lineup should look like against right-handed pitching
- Ben Rice (DH)
- Cody Bellinger (LF)
- Luis García Jr. (1B)
- Heliot Ramos (RF)
- Spencer Jones (CF)
- Jazz Chisholm Jr. (2B)
- George Lombard Jr. (SS)
- Austin Wells (C)
- Ryan McMahon (3B)
This lineup simultaneously features the easiest decisions, but also the roughest circumstances. Having a guy like Judge as the ultimate lineup balancer who mashed both lefties and righties allowed you to use plenty of left-handed hitters at the top of the order, something that the team has in abundance.
The best right-handed hitter on the roster without Judge is hard to pinpoint, especially since all of them are significantly worse against same-handed pitching. Heliot Ramos might just be the best option to bat highest among them, which would be cleanup in this scenario.
It's not an ideal situation in the slightest. Even if you don't think it makes sense to bat Ramos that high because of his struggles against righties, there is some merit to breaking up the team's many left-handed bats. In a lineup that will likely only feature one other righty, it has to be considered.
The fate of this lineup when they're out there, which would likely be mostly after a potential Wild Card Series with the Red Sox, would hinge on the middle. Spencer Jones and Jazz Chisholm Jr. got hot in August and helped the offensive turnaround begin, but both are heavily streaky bats with contact issues. If they go cold, this lineup might limp through games like they did in July.
What the playoff lineup should look like against left-handed pitching
- Paul Goldschmidt (1B)
- Cody Bellinger (LF)
- Heliot Ramos (RF)
- Ben Rice (DH)
- George Lombard Jr. (SS)
- Spencer Jones (CF)
- Jazz Chisholm Jr. (2B)
- Anthony Volpe/José Caballero (3B)
- Austin Wells (C)
Here's where it gets interesting. How far do you lean into the platoons on a team with several players designated to specifically hit lefties, especially against a team that will likely lean heavily on those types of pitchers in Boston?
Many Yankees fans believe that it would be improper to take a guy like García, who is likely the team's second-best pound-for-pound hitter with Judge injured, out of the lineup, but you don't really have a choice here. He's slashing just .238/.274/.363 against lefties, while Goldschmidt has been among the team's best hitters against them for the last two seasons. Add in Rice's improvements against same-handed pitching, and it just needs to be done.
Using him in a different position is also just not happening. He has not played second base, where he was extremely poor, since 2025. The only position he's played this season is first base. If he wasn't so dreadful out there, maybe he could replace Chisholm, a mediocre hitter against lefties in his own right.
Speaking of defense, you might notice the lack of Amed Rosario, and that's intentional. Rosario's use on this roster was almost exclusively predicated on his ability to hit left-handed pitching, but he's been significantly worse at it this season. Add in his truly dreadful defense, and you have a conundrum.
Anthony Volpe is a better hitter than José Caballero, but there are questions about how his arm strength would play at third, where he's also very inexperienced with just three games played in Triple-A. Caballero would probably get the nod here, but he's someone who just plays better off the bench with his speed and versatility.
It's also an aggressive placement for Lombard, batting fifth in his first career playoff game. The results haven't quite been there yet for him, but he's always been significantly better against lefties and should be slid up the lineup and be treated as one of those platoon bats who are there to hit that handedness, even if it might lead to consequences in the bullpen.
Boston is loaded with left-handed pitching from the rotation to the bullpen, so there will be few opportunities to get to a guy like García on the bench. The rest of the bench would be situational with pinch runners and pinch hitters.
Things ultimately look particularly shallow, but is there a chance that some last-minute reinforcements could help out?
Could Trent Grisham or Giancarlo Stanton return to provide relief?
It seems unlikely, especially early in the postseason, but the Yankees are refusing to shut the door on either Trent Grisham's or Giancarlo Stanton's return.
Grisham, who suffered a Grade 2 hamstring strain earlier this month, was revealed to be "pretty far along" in his running program, and Boone said it's not out of the question that he returns in the season's final days, although an exact timeline for that has not been spelled out. If Grisham is physically ready to get back on the field, it would provide a boost, even if he might not be starting over Jones at this point.
Stanton, who's been out since April due to two separate calf strains and a re-aggravation, has continued to hit through his rehab, but hasn't resumed running as of last Sunday. Considering how it took several weeks for him to even get close to back from injury with his running program last time, this likely doesn't put him in play until the ALCS at the earliest.
While Stanton seems significantly less likely to get into a game again this season, there is a path for Grisham. The team could use him and Ramos in a platoon situation to add yet another lefty to the lineup against right-handed pitching. They could also utilize him as a pinch hitter on a larger bench than usual, due to the team's propensity to carry fewer than 13 pitchers in the Wild Card Series.
The real question for Grisham is defensive. While Jones has absolutely looked shaky in center field, the struggles of Grisham out there are well documented. Add in his diminished athleticism and likely balky hamstring straight off an injury, would it be better if the team just chanced it by throwing him in right field when he plays?
He hasn't played the position since a disastrous error lost the Brewers the 2019 Wild Card Game against the Nationals, but playing it at Yankee Stadium is significantly easier than dealing with the spacious center field. Of course, this is something the Yankees would have to determine their willingness to do beforehand and have him practice the position, so what plans they have will be determined by that.
As for Stanton if he's ever medically able to get back? There just might not be any room for him with Rice as the permanent DH. You don't want to take the bat out of either of their hands, and with the team seemingly having to juggle multiple guys coming off soft-tissue injuries, can they afford to use a roster spot for a designated pinch hitter as they did with 2022 Matt Carpenter?

ARIZONA – This one won’t hurt for the next 25 years, but it might sting for the next eight games.
On an evening when the D-backs turned back the clock to honor a World Series celebration that took place on this same diamond, it became the setting for another Yankees walk-off defeat – this one courtesy of Pavin Smith’s pinch-hit homer, sealing a 5-3 loss on Saturday at Chase Field.
Michael Fulmer took the loss, dropping the Yankees (89-65) five games behind the Rays (94-60) in the American League East with eight left to play, dimming their chances of avoiding a best-of-three AL Wild Card Series.
“We’ve got to go on a good run,” Cam Schlittler said. “It’s going to be tough. I think we’ve had opportunities all season to put ourselves ahead, and we haven’t done a great job of that. There’s still a chance, but we’ve got to play our [butts] off a little bit.”
Even with Saturday’s loss, the Yankees have won eight of 11, yet they have been unable to make up ground. The Rays walked off the Red Sox at Tropicana Field earlier Saturday, Tampa Bay’s seventh win in eight contests.
“They’re playing tremendous baseball. It’s tough to climb up in the standings if they keep winning,” Cody Bellinger said. “It’s mathematically pretty tough, but we’ve got to keep on rolling.”
The Yankees are scheduled to host the Rays for a four-game series that begins on Tuesday at Yankee Stadium.
“We sweep, and then it gets interesting,” manager Aaron Boone said. “But you can’t sweep before [Sunday’s] game.”
The sight of Randy Johnson and Curt Schilling draped in purple and gold as they hoisted the championship trophy atop the infield – just as they did that November evening in 2001 – offered a gut punch for Yankees fans who can clearly picture Luis Gonzalez’s hit sailing over a drawn-in infield.
For the next generation, another was delivered later. The frontrunner to win the American League Cy Young Award, Schlittler was dominant early, holding Arizona hitless until Nolan Arenado’s fifth-inning single.
Tim Tawa followed with a bunt back to the mound that Schlittler couldn’t handle cleanly, the ball falling out of his right hand. Four pitches later, Jordan Lawlar laced a two-run triple to the gap in left-center field, giving Arizona its first lead of the game.
Because of Schlittler’s error, both runs were unearned – though that offered no consolation to the right-hander.
“I’ll take the blame for that,” Schlittler said. “I made an error there and let up two runs. That’s baseball, but that one is on me.”
Heliot Ramos and Austin Wells homered in the sixth, but an uncharacteristic loss of command allowed the D-backs to tie the score.
Schlittler threw eight consecutive pitches out of the zone, then Geraldo Perdomo loaded the bases with a bunt single that third baseman Ryan McMahon fielded but couldn’t make a play on.
Corbin Carroll jumped on a high fastball to lift a sac fly off Schlittler, who struck out the next two batters to wrap his outing.
Schlittler finished the evening with a 1.94 ERA, allowing three runs (one earned) and three hits over six innings, walking three and striking out six.
“I felt like I made an adjustment after the second inning,” Schlittler said. “I was missing a couple arm-side. I made a good adjustment and lost the zone there [in the sixth]. Ultimately, it cost me.”
Though Schlittler was dissatisfied with his performance, Boone said he thought the right-hander “threw the ball great.”
“To get us through that sixth, it was a good job there,” Boone said.
Schlittler’s final start of the regular season is lined up to come during the series against Tampa Bay in the Bronx, carrying some statistical weight.
Schlittler has also allowed one earned run or none in 24 starts this season, joining Sandy Koufax (25 in 1963, 24 in 1966) and Bob Gibson (24 in 1968) as the only pitchers in the Live Ball Era with at least 24 starts of one earned run or none in a season (excluding openers).
Yet all the Yankees care about is making those four games mean something in the AL East race.
“Obviously, the goal is to win the division, rest your guys and get those off-days,” Bellinger said. “That’s always goal number one. Ultimately, World Series champions have come out of the Wild Card. We’ll keep on fighting.”

The New York Yankees posted their starting lineup Saturday afternoon for the second game of a three-game set against the Arizona Diamondbacks, and Paul Goldschmidt was not in it.
New York is trying to take the series after a 9-2 win Friday night at Chase Field. Goldschmidt led off that game and finished with a hit, a walk and two runs scored.
The announced order put Ben Rice at designated hitter, Cody Bellinger in left field and Luis García Jr. at first base. Heliot Ramos started in right, George Lombard Jr. at shortstop, Austin Wells behind the plate, Anthony Volpe at second, Ryan McMahon at third and José Caballero in center. Cam Schlittler was listed as the starting pitcher.
Underdog MLB wrote: “Yankees 9/19 B. Rice DH C. Bellinger LF L. García Jr. 1B H. Ramos RF G. Lombard Jr. SS A. Wells C A. Volpe 2B R. McMahon 3B J. Caballero CF C. Schlittler SP.”
Goldschmidt, a seven-time All-Star, is in his second season with the Yankees after signing a one-year deal in February. He entered Saturday hitting .253 with 85 hits, 18 home runs, 50 RBIs, 44 runs and one stolen base in 102 games.
The 39-year-old first baseman spent his first eight big-league seasons in Arizona. He made six straight All-Star teams from 2013 through 2018 while wearing a Diamondbacks uniform.
After leaving Phoenix, Goldschmidt spent six years with the St. Louis Cardinals and won National League Most Valuable Player honors in 2022.
The Yankees sit second in the American League East at 89-64 through 153 games. They have gone 8-2 in their last 10 and trail the Tampa Bay Rays by four games.
Arizona is third in the National League West at 80-74 after 154 games and 4-6 over its last 10.
Manager Aaron Boone has mixed Goldschmidt’s playing time throughout the second half as younger options such as Rice have taken on larger roles. Goldschmidt started Friday after sitting in recent games.
The veteran remains a respected presence in the clubhouse. The Yankees nominated him for the 2026 MLBPAA Heart and Hustle Award earlier this season.
Goldschmidt signed a one-year, $4 million contract with New York this past offseason after hitting .274 with 10 homers and 45 RBIs in 146 games during his first Yankees season.
He has 390 career home runs and 1,282 RBIs across 16 major-league seasons. Career numbers also include a .286 batting average and seven All-Star selections.
Saturday’s game was scheduled for late afternoon local time. A New York win would give the Yankees the series with one game left.
The Diamondbacks have struggled to find consistent production at first base this year after Goldschmidt left the organization years earlier.
New York continues to chase a postseason berth in the final weeks of the regular season. Goldschmidt’s availability as a pinch-hitter or late-inning option remains part of the roster mix even when he does not start.
The lineup change was posted hours before first pitch and immediately circulated among fans tracking the club’s late-season decisions.

With Aaron Judge likely done for the season, the New York Yankees will rely heavily on their other bats to pick up the slack.
One of those will be Jazz Chisholm Jr., who is nearing a return from the injured list with a sprained right thumb. Chisholm, who was putting up an .832 OPS and .367 wOBA since August 4, is expected to be activated during the Yankees' final homestand this coming week. Despite a very disappointing season as a whole, the 28-year-old's improved play is an extremely encouraging sign.
At the same time, Anthony Volpe has taken full advantage of his new opportunity at second base. When Chisholm went down, Volpe's improvements at the plate in Triple-A carried over to the major leagues and his production from the bottom of the order is a boon to the Yankees' offense. The 25-year old is slashing .296/.345/.481 in 29 plate appearances while also stealing four bases.
The problem is that the Yankees have three middle infielders looking for starting spots. George Lombard Jr. is firmly entrenched at shortstop, which necessitated Volpe's transition to second base. Of course, second base is Chisholm's natural position and the Yankees have gotten well-above average defense from him there.
This means one of these three will be the odd man out... or does it?
The Yankees should play Jazz Chisholm Jr. at third base again
When the Yankees acquired Chisholm at the trade deadline in 2024, they already had Gleyber Torres at second base. So they tested Chisholm out at third base to ensure both players would be in the starting lineup. Chisholm also saw time at the hot corner last year when DJ LeMahieu played second, until the Yankees eventually released the aging LeMahieu to move Chisholm back to his natural position.
Chisholm's defense suffered at third in 2025, as he was worth -3 Outs Above Average (per Baseball Savant). But his athleticism and dynamic skillset is far too great to leave him out of the lineup entirely, even if he's endured a down year. On the other hand, it would be foolish for the Yankees to sit Volpe while he's hot at the plate and adapting well to second.
While second base has two strong options, third base is a major weakness. Ryan McMahon has been atrocious since returning to the lineup on Sept. 1, hitting just .154/.214/.179 in 42 plate appearances; the abysmal offensive production far outweighs McMahon's steady defense, even if the Yankees are going to rely on run prevention in the postseason. Jose Caballero is also capable of playing third, but he's best suited as a bench player at this point.
Between Chisholm and Volpe, the former is better suited to play third due to his past experience. The latter has a grand total of three games and 22.0 innings at the hot corner, all of them in Triple-A.
This certainly isn't an ideal situation for Chisholm: he's struggled for much of the season, got injured when he started turning things around, and may need to play at a secondary position to accommodate a teammate.
But this would likely be the Yankees' best lineup without Aaron Judge, and if Chisholm wants to both win a World Series and secure a future in the Bronx, then moving over to third is the best thing he can do to help the team right now.

item.content:encoded:
The two starting pitchers entered this game trending in opposite directions. Gerrit Cole had just allowed the most home runs (seven) in a two-start span in his career, while Eduardo Rodriguez is in the midst of a career year with a 2.62 ERA. One of those trends remained — Cole giving up another home run on a fastball — but fortunately the other trend was momentarily halted, the Yankees scoring five in the first off E-Rod to give themselves enough of a cushion to weather Cole’s continued home run woes.
Cole settled down after the Carroll dinger to give the Yankees six innings, by which time the offense all but put this game out of reach. They kept the pressure on, scoring a further four runs including solo home runs by Ben Rice and George Lombard Jr., to cruise to a series-opening victory in the desert, 9-2.
Rodriguez came into this game with an ERA above six in the first inning and an ERA right around two for the subsequent innings combined. That made it imperative that the Yankees find a way to do damage before the home team had a chance to come to bat, especially with the rate Cole is giving up the long ball. They did just that with a clear disciplined approach not to expand the zone against E-Rod’s curveball.
Paul Goldschmidt drew a leadoff walk, Cody Bellinger followed with a single, and Heliot Ramos also walked to load the bases with no outs. Rice drew the Yankees’ third walk in the first four batters to plate Goldschmidt and open the scoring, Goldy, Ramos, and Rice all working full counts before taking the free pass. Amed Rosario then fought off a cutter that handcuffed him up and in, muscling it to the opposite field perfectly between center and left fielder to plate Bellinger as the runners went station to station. A wild pitch allowed Ramos to score and Rice and Rosario to move up to second and third. This set up a two-run ground ball single from Lombard that just got by Geraldo Perdomo’s diving attempt to atone for his defensive misplay in the 13th that allowed the Twins to walk off the Yankees on Wednesday.
Rodriguez struck out Volpe to end the inning giving him three strikeouts in the frame, but the damage was done. The 45 pitches he threw were the most he’s thrown in the first inning in his career. 33 of those pitches fell out of the zone, but only eight induced a chase.
It’s a good thing they hung such a crooked number, because Cole immediately gave two of those runs back. He gave up a leadoff single to Perdomo before yanking an 0-1 four-seamer right into Corbin Carroll’s nitro zone, the three-time All-Star obliterating it to right for a two-run bomb to reduce the Yankees’ lead, 5-2. Rice made sure to immediately tilt the momentum back in his team’s favor. After falling behind 0-2, he stayed back on an elevated heater from E-Rod riding it out the other way and over the fence in left-center for a leadoff bomb, his 39th of the year, to give Cole some more of his cushion back, 6-2.
Cole settled down to work a scoreless third and fourth, helped in part by a sharp uptick in slider usage at the expense of some four-seamers as well as an impressive sliding catch in left-center by Spencer Jones in the third. He finally began dialing the fastball command to the corners in the fifth, striking out Tim Tawa and Lars Nootbaar on four-seamers to end the frame after Jesús Sánchez singled with one out. This allowed Lombard to restore the Yankees’ five run lead in the sixth, the rookie punishing a hanging curveball from E-Rod by lining the solo shot down the line it left and into the bullpen for his fourth of the year and third RBI on the night.
The four-seamer was the prime culprit for Cole in his previous two starts with a 68.2-percent hard-hit rate and just six whiffs, and that remained the case tonight. However, I believe it is Cole’s rustiness with his secondaries that is leading his four-seamer to get barreled. The fastball still has plenty of velocity — at 97 mph it’s a full tick above last season. I will grant that he has missed location in the zone on numerous occasions which hasn’t done him any favors.
However, after his last start, Cole identified a lack of chase and whiff against his secondaries as the reason his fastball is getting crushed. Hitters being able to lay off those chase pitches forces Cole to overuse the fastball in counts that favor the softer stuff, which in essence gives them the opportunity to hunt the heater when they should be defending against the breaker. When you can hunt a fastball in any count, chances are you are going to do damage when Cole misses his spot in the zone, the high velocity not much of a weapon when hitters’ bats are preemptively sped up.
Indeed, once he started commanding his slider and knuckle curve to the shadow of the zone in the middle innings, the hard contact against the fastball dried up. Having pitched a strong fifth and sixth and with his pitch count at 90, Boone saw no reason to overextend Cole and ended his night after six with his best innings freshest in mind. He finished night having pitched six innings, allowing two runs on four hits with no walks and six strikeouts.
Despite possessing one of the stingiest bullpens in baseball, the Diamondbacks decided that a five-run deficit in the seventh was too steep to justify using their high leverage arms. So, Zac Gallen made his first career relief appearance, the former All-Star in the midst of am injury-plagued, below-replacement-level campaign. He allowed a leadoff single to Goldschmidt and walked Ramos and Rice — again, both in full counts — to load the bases with one out. Aaron Boone sent out Ryan McMahon to pinch-hit for Rosario, and he hit a sharp grounder to first that Pavin Smith gloved but airmailed the underhand toss to Gallen covering first as all the runners were safe and a run scored on the error. Spencer Jones then appeared to ground into the inning-ending double play, but his hustle out of the box and down the line just beat the throw to pick up an RBI and make it 9-2.
Ryan Yarbrough pitched 1.1 innings in relief of Cole and worked himself into and out of trouble in the seventh. Arizona put runners on second and third as Nolan Arenado singled and Carroll doubled with one out. However, Yarbrough struck out Jose Fernandez and Tawa to strand the pair in scoring position. Rice smoked his fourth triple of the year in the ninth but was stranded at third by a McMahon strikeout. Michael Fulmer and Luis Gil recorded the final five outs of the game without allowing a baserunner to seal the win, 9-2. With the Rays having lost to the Red Sox earlier in the evening, the Yankees’ deficit is back to four games in the division, making that looming four-game set against Tampa in the Bronx even more high stakes.
Cam Schlittler looks to cement his AL Cy Young case tomorrow after Dylan Cease suffered his shortest start of the season on Friday. The Yankees ace will face off against Brandon Pfaadt with a slightly more reasonable game start time. First pitch is scheduled for 8:10 pm ET with the broadcast remaining on YES.
Yankees rout the D-Backs, 9-2, who's your Player of the Game?
Gerrit Cole pitched 6 innings of 2-run ball. George Lombard Jr. hit a two-run single and a solo homer. Ben Rice raked with a solo homer, triple, and two walks.

The New York Yankees could make a surprising move on Anthony Volpe.
Volpe has had success since being recalled, but George Lombard Jr. has taken over as the starting shortstop. So, Volpe's future in New York is very much up in the air.
New York will begin a three-game road series against the Arizona Diamondbacks on Friday.
New York Yankees Surprise Anthony Volpe Decision
Although Volpe has been playing better, he isn't guaranteed a spot on the Yankees playoff roster.
After New York clinched a playoff spot, Yankees analysts Bryan Hoch and Patrick Donnelly of MLB.com revealed the likely playoff roster, and they didn't have Volpe on it.
What could the postseason roster look like?
C: Austin Wells, Ali Sánchez
1B: Luis García Jr., Paul Goldschmidt
2B: Jazz Chisholm Jr.
3B: Ryan McMahon, Amed Rosario
SS: George Lombard Jr., José Caballero
OF: Cody Bellinger, Spencer Jones, Aaron Judge, Heliot Ramos
DH: Ben Rice
SP: Cam Schlittler, Max Fried, Gerrit Cole
RP: David Bednar, Brent Headrick, Paul Blackburn, Tim Hill, Ryan Yarbrough, Clarke Schmidt, Michael Fulmer, Ryan Weathers, Will Warren
The Yankees leaving Volpe off the playoff roster would be a disappointing outcome for the shortstop. It also could signal the end of his tenure in New York as Lombard is the shortstop of the future.
Volpe is hitting .253 with 2 home runs and 26 RBIs this season with the Yankees.
New York Right Now
The Yankees have clinched a playoff spot as New York will be hosting a Wild Card series again.
"Every year you go through a lot, it seems like. But we've been through a lot this year with injuries, with adversity," Yankees manager Aaron Boone said. "But credit to them for coming together. Through all the ups and downs, they've been a together group. I feel like they've developed a lot of grit over the season."
However, despite clinching a playoff spot, the Yankees made it clear the job isn't finished. New York likely won't win the AL East again, which is frustrating, but the Yankees have confidence they can go on a deep playoff run.
The Yankees are 88-64 and 5 games back of the Tampa Bay Rays for the top spot in the AL East.

item.content:encoded:
Es común pensar en los Yankees como un equipo experimentado en los playoffs. Después de todo, ésta es la octava vez en nueve años que han llegado a la postemporada bajo la dirección del manager Aaron Boone. Y una rápida mirada a algunos de sus jugadores principales muestra una alineación que varía entre un poco y una gran cantidad de experiencia en octubre.
Jugador, Número de Partidos de Playoffs de por vida
Cody Bellinger, 76
Aaron Judge, 65
Paul Goldschmidt, 29
Trent Grisham, 26
Jazz Chisholm, Jr. 24
Austin Wells, 21
Anthony Volpe, 21
Amed Rosario, 11
Ryan McMahon, 10
Ben Rice, 6
José Caballero, 3
Pero faltan algunos nombres en esa lista: El campocorto George Lombard Jr., el jardinero Spencer Jones, el primera base dominicano Luis García Jr. y el jardinero puertorriqueño Heliot Ramos. Ninguno de esos cuatro nunca ha jugado en la postemporada, ya sea con los Yankees o, como es el caso de García y Ramos, con sus equipos anteriores.
Ahora, es posible que algunos de los jugadores veteranos lesionados -- Grisham y Chisholm, específicamente -- puedan regresar a la alineación y enviar a algunos de esos nuevos rostros a la banca o fuera del roster de postemporada por completo. Pero es seguro decir que los Yankees van a contar con al menos algunos novatos en los playoffs el próximo mes, en su búsqueda de ganar su primera Serie Mundial desde el 2009.
Boone ha expresado que sus jóvenes y los recién llegados a los playoffs tienen otra ventaja sobre los jugadores en otros mercados.
"Jugar para los Yankees, jugar en Nueva York”, dijo, "tiene una manera de prepararte para la postemporada”.
Éste ha sido un año de transición en las Grandes Ligas. Consulta la primera ronda del Draft del 2023 si quieres pruebas. No menos de 19 de las 37 selecciones de primera ronda y de compensación han debutado en las Mayores, y muchos de ellos ya son jugadores clave en sus equipos.
"Los jugadores están llegando a las Grandes Ligas a un ritmo muy rápido ahora y a temprana edad”, manifestó el piloto de los Tigers, A.J. Hinch, quien ha dado la bienvenida a la tercera selección Max Clark y al favorito para Novato del Año de la Liga Americana, Kevin McGonigle, a Detroit este año. "No creo que se sientan tan impresionados por los grandes pasos que están dando”.
Para los Yankees, ese grupo incluye a Lombard, quien se ha aclimatado bien desde que fue subido a principios de agosto. Y Jones fue elogiado recientemente nada menos que por Aaron Judge, quien dijo que el jardinero novato "realmente ha evolucionado cada vez que ha sido subido, mejorando un poco más en cada ocasión”.
Por supuesto, habrá contratiempos en el camino. El miércoles, Jones se fue de 6-0 con cinco ponches y cometió un error cuando dejó caer un batazo en el jardín central. Y Lombard no pudo atrapar un roletazo del boricua Victor Caratini en la 13ª entrada que fue considerado un sencillo mientras los Mellizos vencían a los Yankees.
Pero cualquiera que siga el béisbol sabe que los días malos y las malas jugadas son parte del ciclo de crecimiento de un jugador de Grandes Ligas. La clave es aprender de ellos para poder limitarlos en el futuro. Y todo ello -- lo bueno, lo malo y lo ocasionalmente feo -- ayuda a preparar a un joven jugador para su primera vez jugando en el béisbol de octubre.
El mundo está a punto de descubrir lo preparados que están los Yankees jóvenes. Pero Jones ofreció un poco de tranquilidad el lunes mientras disfrutaba de la celebración en el vestuario después de la victoria en Target Field que aseguró otra clasificación de Nueva York para los playoffs.
"Creo que para nosotros, jugamos mejor cuando la multitud se vuelve más ruidosa", dijo. "Estoy bien emocionado por lo que está por venir”.

item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees could make a surprising decision on veteran infielder Ryan McMahon before the playoffs.
New York clinched a playoff berth. They will likely be in the Wild Card series again, likely playing the Boston Red Sox for the second year in a row.
The Yankees are 88-64.
New York Yankees Could Bench Ryan McMahon
With the Yankees heading back to the playoffs, New York could have to make a difficult decision on veteran infielder Ryan McMahon.
McMahon is a solid glove-first third baseman, but he has struggled offensively since coming to New York. With that, Yankees analyst Pat Ragazzo of FanSided believes New York could remove McMahon from its playoff roster, or simply have him on the bench.
"Should Rosario's hot streak continue into the end of the regular season, the Yankees find a way to utilize him at third base during the postseason," Ragazzo wrote. "There's even a world where Jose Caballero slides to third, with Anthony Volpe available off the bench. McMahon will probably still get a roster spot, but they cannot play his bat regularly in the biggest games of the year. McMahon's bat creates a black hole in the Yankees' lineup, which they cannot afford to deploy in October.
"If not for his defense, McMahon would've likely been designated for assignment by now. And given his historically poor offensive numbers, it seems like it could be headed that way with McMahon under contract for another year at $16 million. The 31-year-old just has not worked out as a member of the Yankees. His time in pinstripes should come to an end sooner rather than later."
McMahon has one more year on his six-year, $70 million deal. Not having him on the playoff roster would be a tough look. Yet, his bat has struggled, and the Yankees could use Caballero at third, with Volpe as the primary backup infielder in the playoffs.
McMahon is hitting .210 with 10 home runs and 34 RBIs this season.
New York Right Now
The Yankees have clinched a playoff spot and once again have World Series aspirations.
Although New York did clinch a playoff spot, the Yankees know the job is not done.
"Every year you go through a lot, it seems like. But we've been through a lot this year with injuries, with adversity," Yankees manager Aaron Boone said. "But credit to them for coming together. Through all the ups and downs, they've been a together group. I feel like they've developed a lot of grit over the season."
The Yankees are set to begin a three-game road series against the Arizona Diamondbacks on Friday.

item.content:encoded:
PHOENIX — Los Yankees se han pasado todo el mes de septiembre intentando convertir su clasificación para la postemporada en una plantilla más clara de cara a octubre. Una de sus decisiones más difíciles de tomar ahora mismo tiene que ver con la tercera base.
Ryan McMahon llegó como un jugador que aportaba estabilidad sobre todo en defensa, pero cada vez le cuesta más ocultar su bateo. Su último bache se produjo el miércoles en el Target Field, donde se fue de 0 de 6 con cuatro strikeouts en la derrota por 5-4, en 13 entradas, ante los Minnesota Twins.
Los Yankees no dejaron de remontar. Anthony Volpe empató el partido con un doble en la novena entrada. Ali Sánchez puso a Nueva York por delante en la décima, y José Caballero sumó un fly de sacrificio en la undécima. Minnesota respondió en cada ocasión hasta que Víctor Caratini sentenció el partido con un sencillo decisivo en la 13.ª. Tommy Nance se llevó la victoria, John Schreiber la derrota y no hubo salvamento.
McMahon, que bateaba séptimo, terminó la noche con un promedio de .210/.275/.346, 10 jonrones y 34 carreras impulsadas en 118 partidos. Se ha puesto a cero 101 veces, lo que supone un porcentaje del 29,2 %, mientras que su OPS es de .621. Las estadísticas avanzadas actuales que acompañan a las críticas le sitúan en un wRC+ de 77 y un fWAR de 0,5.
Este momento hace que cada turno al bate sin resultado se note más. Los Yankees llegaban al viernes con un balance de 88-64, a cinco partidos de Tampa Bay en la División Este de la Liga Americana, con la clasificación para la postemporada ya asegurada. Jazz Chisholm Jr. sigue en la lista de lesionados de 10 días por un esguince en el pulgar derecho, mientras que Volpe ha vuelto de la Triple A y ha jugado como segunda base.
La trayectoria de Volpe en las ligas menores ha ampliado las opciones de los Yankees. Durante su etapa en la Triple A, jugó como shortstop, segunda base y tercera base. Eso no significa que sea la solución definitiva para la tercera base, pero le da a Aaron Boone otra opción de alineación que tener en cuenta cuando vuelva Chisholm.
McMahon también tiene un sueldo garantizado de 16 millones de dólares para 2027. Los Yankees tienen que decidir si su defensa y su contrato siguen justificando que sea titular cuando la diferencia en ataque se ha vuelto tan grande.
McMahon entra en la zona de peligro de LeMahieu
Esa combinación ha hecho que cada vez más gente de los Yankees se plantee una pregunta más dura: si McMahon debería perder su puesto de titular, quedar fuera de la plantilla de la postemporada o, al final, ser designado para cesión.
La comparación que está cobrando fuerza es la de DJ LeMahieu, a quien los Yankees dejaron libre en julio de 2025 cuando aún le quedaban por cobrar unos 22 millones de dólares. Según FanGraphs, en su última temporada con los Yankees, LeMahieu registró un wRC+ de 94, un porcentaje de embasado de 0,338 y una tasa de strikeouts del 24,6 %.
McMahon está por debajo de todos esos indicadores ofensivos. Su porcentaje de llegada a base de 0,275 y su tasa de strikeouts del 29,2 % hacen que los Yankees obtengan menos aportación ofensiva de la que recibían de LeMahieu antes de decidir que ya no encajaba en su plantilla.
Las situaciones no son iguales. LeMahieu tenía 36 años, su papel se había reducido y Nueva York quería a Chisholm en segunda base. McMahon es más joven y sigue aportando valor en tercera base. Pero la decisión sobre LeMahieu dejó claro que el dinero garantizado no siempre protege el puesto de un veterano en la plantilla.
Boone sigue centrándose en el grupo
Los Yankees no han dicho públicamente que McMahon vaya a quedar fuera de la plantilla. Tras asegurarse el título, Boone habló de cómo el vestuario había afrontado una temporada difícil, en lugar de dar a entender que se hubiera tomado ninguna decisión sobre un veterano.
«Pero hay que reconocerles el mérito de haberse mantenido unidos. A pesar de todos los altibajos, han sido un grupo muy unido», dijo Boone.
Ese comentario no aclara cuál será el papel de McMahon en octubre. Lo que sí hace es resaltar la diferencia entre las presiones externas para que lo echen y la decisión que los Yankees hayan tomado realmente.
La defensa ya no es la respuesta definitiva
El argumento más sólido de McMahon sigue siendo su guante. La instantánea que te he pasado muestra un DRS de -1 y un Fielding Run Value de +1, mientras que la página en directo de Statcast muestra un valor defensivo global ligeramente positivo. La cifra exacta varía según la métrica y el momento de la actualización, pero la ventaja defensiva no oculta un OPS de 0,621.
Un tercera base con un OPS de 0,621 puede seguir siendo una opción válida si su defensa es de primera y el resto de la alineación está en forma. Los Yankees tienen menos margen mientras Chisholm esté de baja, y en octubre cada puesto de la alineación cobra más importancia.
Volpe no es un tercera base contrastado en las Grandes Ligas, y los Yankees no han dado a entender que tengan pensado darle esa posición. Aun así, su reciente actuación en esa posición en la Triple A le da a Boone una alternativa real. Su experiencia como campocorto hace que la objeción sobre la potencia de su brazo no sea tan sencilla, pero eso no garantiza que vaya a defender bien la tercera base en octubre.
La comparación de Okamoto hay que ponerla en contexto
Otra comparación que circula entre los aficionados de los Yankees compara a McMahon con el tercera base de Toronto, Kazuma Okamoto. Según la MLB, Okamoto tiene un promedio de bateo de 0,235, con 33 jonrones, 88 carreras impulsadas y un OPS de 0,774. Su contrato de cuatro años y 60 millones de dólares tiene un valor medio anual de 15 millones de dólares.
McMahon gana 16 millones de dólares y lleva 10 jonrones con un OPS de 0,621. A primera vista, el contraste es enorme.
No se trata de una decisión de la directiva en la que se pueda comparar a uno con otro sin más. McMahon ya tenía contrato cuando los Yankees lo ficharon en 2025, mientras que Okamoto llegó a la MLB siguiendo un camino diferente como agente libre. Aun así, la comparación salarial ayuda a entender por qué se han intensificado las críticas y por qué algunas de ellas se han extendido hasta el director general, Brian Cashman.
Octubre obliga a los Yankees a decidirse por un papel
No hay indicios confirmados de que los Yankees hayan decidido designar a McMahon para cesión o sacarlo de la plantilla de la postemporada. Sigue en activo, y la incertidumbre sobre la fecha de regreso de Chisholm hace que la situación en el cuadro siga siendo incierta.
Pero la cuestión ya no es si McMahon está pasando por una mala racha. Es cuánto tiempo de juego pueden permitirse los Yankees darle a un bateador con un wRC+ de 77 cuando empiece octubre.

item.content:encoded:
NUEVA YORK — El cántico empezó de forma discreta y se extendió rápidamente. «The Fox» está en racha. Dos palabras para un jugador que pasó la mayor parte del verano en un segundo plano, enviado a las ligas menores y al que casi habían descartado de los planes de los Yankees. Ahora no se le va a sacar de la alineación, y ese es precisamente el problema.
Hace un mes, pocos habrían imaginado que Anthony Volpe iba a ser importante este septiembre. Había perdido su puesto de campocorto, había aceptado un descenso de categoría y había visto cómo un novato ocupaba su antigua posición. Su regreso parecía una simple nota al pie de una temporada perdida.
En cambio, se ha colado de lleno en una decisión que los Yankees no esperaban tener que tomar. Su bate es impresionante, su guante es impecable y su llegada no podría ser más inoportuna para un entrenador que está intentando cerrar la plantilla para octubre.
El problema es dónde juega, no cómo juega. Y el jugador al que está desplazando no ha hecho nada malo.
Desde que volvió a los Yankees el 10 de septiembre, Volpe lleva 8 de 23 con un jonrón, dos dobles, siete carreras impulsadas y cuatro bases robadas en siete partidos, con un promedio de bateo de .348 y un OPS de .965, además de haber sido titular seis veces en la segunda base.
Esa racha ha complicado bastante la situación en el cuadro interior a falta de 10 partidos, ya que la segunda base es de Jazz Chisholm Jr., que se espera que vuelva de la lista de lesionados antes de los playoffs. Los Yankees están a cuatro partidos de Tampa Bay en la División Este de la Liga Americana y luchan por el primer puesto de comodín de la Liga Americana.
Un descenso de categoría que parece un punto de inflexión
El reinicio empezó en agosto, cuando los Yankees enviaron a Volpe a la Triple A de Scranton/Wilkes-Barre. Parecía que lo habían dejado en el banquillo. Quizá fuera una estrategia.
Volpe arrasó en la Liga Internacional, registrando un OPS de 0,906 tras el descenso y bateando para 0,440 con un porcentaje de embasado de 0,533 en septiembre, antes de que lo volvieran a llamar. Llegó al Bronx como un bateador muy diferente al que se había ido.
El cambio fue mecánico, no solo mental. Volpe analizó vídeos antiguos, descartó su patrón de movimiento anterior y añadió un pequeño paso hacia atrás con el pie derecho para mejorar su sincronización y equilibrio. Este reajuste hizo que la longitud de su swing se redujera de 7,1 pies a 6,8 pies, y la tasa de golpes bien alineados de Volpe se disparó del 30,6 % al 47,1 %.
El regreso fue por todo lo alto. En su primer partido tras su vuelta, el 10 de septiembre, Volpe conectó 3 de 4 con un grand slam y cinco carreras impulsadas —su mejor marca personal— en la goleada de los Yankees a Colorado.
El problema de Chisholm que nadie había previsto
Chisholm entró en la lista de lesionados el 9 de septiembre con un esguince en el pulgar derecho, que se hizo al deslizarse de cabeza hacia la segunda base la noche anterior. Los Yankees te lo han dejado fuera de la actividad deportiva entre siete y diez días, y tienes un historial de recuperarte rápido.
Ese regreso es el problema. Chisholm es el segunda base titular, y su puesto no está en duda. Cuando está en forma, vuelve a ocupar la posición en la que Volpe está jugando tan bien ahora.
Así que los Yankees se enfrentan a un dilema. Volpe está rindiendo bien en el puesto de Chisholm, el tercera base Ryan McMahon no está pasando por su mejor momento y el novato George Lombard Jr. ocupa el puesto de campocorto. Es posible que alguien que tenga motivos para jugar acabe en el banquillo.
El entrenador Aaron Boone no ha dado pistas sobre cómo se repartirán los turnos al bate cuando Chisholm vuelva a estar disponible. Sin embargo, se ha mostrado muy elogioso con el esfuerzo que ha hecho Volpe para recuperarse.
«Le tengo un respeto enorme, tanto como persona como jugador», dijo Boone. «Ha sido todo un profesional y se ha esforzado al máximo en todo lo que le han echado encima».
La cifra que cambia el enfoque del debate
Este es el detalle que cambia el tema de conversación, y que pocos han destacado. Volpe ha estado casi impecable en una posición en la que no había jugado desde 2021. Hasta el miércoles, solo había cometido un error en 162 1/3 entradas en la segunda base, con un porcentaje de fildeo de 0,987.
Eso importa porque lo que se le echaba en cara a Volpe nunca fue su guante como shortstop. Era su bate. Si su defensa sigue igual y su swing se mantiene, los Yankees ya no estarán sopesando una racha de buena forma frente a una mala racha. Los Yankees estarán sopesando a dos jugadores útiles para un número cada vez más reducido de plazas en la plantilla.
A Boone le ha gustado lo que mostraban los informes de desarrollo, incluido el trabajo de Volpe en la doble jugada.
«Es el tipo de deportista al que le debería ir bien en esa posición», dijo Boone. «No me sorprende».
Una vieja polémica con un nuevo giro
Hay algo de ironía en este camino de vuelta. En julio, un informe afirmaba que Volpe se había negado a jugar de segunda base, una historia que tanto él como los Yankees desmintieron y por cuya difusión el comentarista Michael Kay se disculpó públicamente. Ahora, la segunda base se ha convertido precisamente en el camino que devuelve a Volpe a la primera línea.
Su versatilidad es la historia paralela que pasa desapercibida en los Yankees. La Triple A le preparó para jugar en segunda y tercera base, además de en el campo corto, lo que le da a Boone opciones que el bate de McMahon no se ha ganado. McMahon tiene un promedio de bateo de 0,210 con un OPS de 0,621 en 118 partidos, aunque su defensa en tercera base sigue siendo sólida.
En el panorama general de los Yankees , lo mejor sigue siendo tener paciencia. Chisholm vuelve a la segunda base, Lombard se queda en el campo corto y Boone se encargará de gestionar la rotación día a día. Pero Volpe ha convertido una convocatoria de emergencia en una auténtica prueba, y no deja de complicar una decisión que, en principio, sería fácil.
Para un jugador de los Yankees que en agosto parecía prescindible, eso ya es una victoria en sí misma. Los Yankees buscaban profundidad para septiembre. En cambio, se llevaron una decisión.
