item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees have a lot of decisions to make for their postseason roster, from lineup construction to the outfield, rotation, and bullpen, to managing guys coming back from injury. Outside of the team's core foundation, almost nothing is settled, especially on the bubble.
One of those bubble spots entails the backup infielders behind a hopefully healthy Jazz Chisholm Jr., George Lombard Jr., and Ryan McMahon. As of right now, the Yankees have three of them on the roster: Jos Caballero, Amed Rosario, and Anthony Volpe. The former has a secured spot due to his speed and versatility, but the latter two aren't as secure.
It's entirely possible the Yankees carry 14 position players on the playoff roster, but that means somebody will have to go for Chisholm when he returns. It's widely believed the corresponding move will be to send Volpe back to the minors, but what if the Yankees went another direction?
Here's why Volpe should be the one who lands that final infield spot instead of Rosario, and how the Yankees can handle the roster math:
New look Anthony Volpe can provide value to Yankees
I am personally not drinking the Kool-Aid of any tangible offensive improvements for Volpe, at least in the short term. What he did at Triple-A was feast on inferior pitchers with his opposite-field approach, something that doesn't have a 1-to-1 conversion rate in the big leagues. That said, we know what he is throughout his career: a mediocre hitter with a career 84 OPS+ and an 89 OPS+ this season in 62 games entering Wednesday.
That said, the ability to hit is maybe the least important aspect for a bench player, particularly one on a team that will have pinch-hitting options on both sides of the plate but needs defenders to replace them.
Volpe was not a fit for this roster when he only played shortstop, something that he would no longer get a chance to do with Lombard entrenched at the position. Upon his demotion to Triple-A, he got experience at second and third base, with the former being the position he's played almost every day since he was recalled after Chisholm's injury. Early returns are positive there.
At this point, we can directly compare Volpe to Rosario, who has also predominantly played second and third base when he has played. While offense is likely not on the 25-year-old's side, defense and baserunning certainly are. He's a vastly superior defender, posting a 3 DRS, 5 FRV, and 5 OAA at shortstop earlier this season.
Volpe is also a much more aggressive baserunner, recording 10 stolen bases and being one of baseball's best at stealing third base, an extremely critical skill to have in close playoff games.
And all of this assumes that Volpe's bat remains as bad as it's been throughout his career. But what if he did make positive adjustments? What if this new approach, coupled with his improved plate discipline from Opening Day, makes him playable, even as a platoon bat? He's already had a few clutch hits, as we saw in the Twins' series.
Amed Rosario's 2026 struggles make him expendable
The one thing that Rosario has on Volpe is his hitting ability, particularly against left-handed pitching, but we've gotten enough samples this season to determine whether a player's reputation actually backs up the results. For Rosario? It's not pretty.
A career .287 hitter against lefties, Rosario is down to just .200 with a .602 OPS against them in 151 plate appearances, something that goes beyond a small sample size. His strikeout rate against them at 21.1 percent is the highest it's been in a decade, while his quality of contact has similarly tanked, even if he's been very unlucky (.262 wOBA vs. .306 xwOBA). Compare this to Volpe, who's slashing a mediocre (but better) .253/.323/.373 against lefties this season, so is Rosario's best strength now a weakness?
He's had pretty hefty reverse splits this season, which completely goes against why he was signed. The Yankees have significantly better options on both sides of the ball against righties, so it doesn't help them at all. When you factor in his defensive shortcomings? He really seems like someone who should be on the chopping block.
Rosario is a guy who can play corner outfield and three infield positions, but plays none of them well. In just 303 innings this season at third base, he has -8 OAA and -7 FRV. He's also managed to be minor negatives in just 48 combined innings in left field, right field, and second base. On a rate basis, he's arguably the worst defender in baseball, something that would be muted if his bat was going (or if the DH spot was more accessible).
He's not a bad baserunner at all. In fact, he's one of the faster guys on the team in terms of sprint speed, but the few times he's on base this season, he's rarely in motion. He has just three stolen bases in the last two seasons and has been a net-negative baserunner according to Baseball Savant's Baserunning Runs metric due to a lack of aggressiveness in taking the extra base.
When your one strength isn't much of a strength anymore, and your usage on the roster is diminished, it has us asking how Volpe could help the team with its roster construction in the postseason.
How the roster shakes out
It wouldn't even be a major roster disruptor. Rosario is almost always the last guy on the bench because of how little the team trusts him defensively. If his bat was that much of an upgrade in a platoon situation, they'd make that trade, but it hasn't.
Come playoff time, I can see a world where the Yankees play Volpe at second or third base in place of McMahon or Chisholm against a left-handed pitcher to increase the at-bat quality without a massive defensive drop-off. It would also give them another pinch-running option they might need in late and close situations, as one of the best base stealers on the team.
I don't expect the Yankees to want to get rid of Rosario, though. He can be left off the playoff roster without a problem. But he can't be removed before then, which could cause an issue if Chisholm is likely to return before the postseason begins.
Therefore, a potential solution could be to send a pitcher down and play with an extra position player down the stretch, but the team is running out of players with options. Volpe could also go down just to fit puzzle pieces and return a few days later.
Ultimately, whatever the Yankees decide, it might not be the difference between a playoff series or even a playoff game, but margins are margins. This has not been a team that has won enough close games late, so giving yourself as much of an advantage in those situations is paramount.

The New York Yankees will have a decision to make when Jazz Chisholm Jr. is back from the injured list.
Anthony Volpe is up in Chisholm's place, but he is looking like a completely different hitter after a stint in Triple-A. He has made some changes and is hitting .348/.400/.565 with a home run, two doubles, four stolen bases and seven RBIs. Before he was optioned, he had a .240 batting average and a .646 OPS with one home run in 56 games.
When Chisholm is back, he will go back to starting every day. Even though it's a down year for him, he had really turned things around before his injury. Before his injury, Chisholm was slashing .313/.398/.835 and had 10 stolen bases since Aug. 9.
If Volpe stays hot, the Yankees cannot really afford to keep him out of the lineup. On the other hand, they cannot bench Chisholm, who was swinging it well and has been a starter all year. What can they do then? Well, the Brewers could leave Volpe at second base and play Chisholm at third base.
Ryan McMahon has not been great at third base, and if Chisholm is swinging the bat like he was for a month before his injury, he would easily be the best option there. He is not as strong a defender there, but the Yankees would be much better offensively without McMahon in the lineup.
Of course, this is dependent on Volpe staying hot and Chisholm picking up where he left off. If both of those don't happen, it becomes a situation where the Yankees need to pick one or the other, and it seems like Chisholm would get the nod.

Ryan McMahon's tenure with the New York Yankees hasn't gone as planned. He has certainly been a strong fielder at third base (though not as exceptional as he was sold), but his bat has been anemic by any metric. So much so that after going 0-for-6 with four strikeouts on Wednesday, he has officially joined similar territory as a number of infamous Yankees who underperformed during their time in pinstripes.
As pointed out by Jack Fungo on X, McMahon has a 80 wRC+ in 162 games since being acquired by the Yankees at the 2025 trade deadline. That is a lower mark than DJ LeMahieu's final season with the Yankees when he got released, Josh Donaldson's career in the Bronx, Joey Gallo's time with the Yankees, Isiah Kiner-Falefa's 2023 season and Anthony Volpe's 2025 season.
Ryan McMahon's Yankees company proves the DFA bells are tolling
This isn't great company to be in for McMahon. To put things in perspective, McMahon is 20 points below the league average of 100 for wRC+. On the season, McMahon has hit 10 home runs, has driven in 34 RBI and sports a .210/.275/.346 slash line with a .621 OPS.
McMahon had some solid offensive years with the Colorado Rockies in his career, but his home splits were always much better due to his numbers at Coors Field being inflated as a result of the high altitude. The writing appeared to be on the wall for McMahon before he switched cities.
But the Yankees traded for McMahon because they were desperate for a third baseman last year. They also landed Amed Rosario to platoon with McMahon at the hot corner. Neither has stepped up to claim the job on an everyday basis, though Rosario's bat has been markedly better lately (.348 average in his last seven sporadically placed games).
Should Rosario's hot streak continue into the end of the regular season, the Yankees find a way to utilize him at third base during the postseason. There's even a world where Jose Caballero slides to third, with Anthony Volpe available off the bench. McMahon will probably still get a roster spot, but they cannot play his bat regularly in the biggest games of the year. McMahon's bat creates a black hole in the Yankees' lineup, which they cannot afford to deploy in October.
If not for his defense, McMahon would've likely been designated for assignment by now. And given his historically poor offensive numbers, it seems like it could be headed that way with McMahonunder contract for another year at $16 million. The 31-year-old just has not worked out as a member of the Yankees, and his time in pinstripes should come to an end sooner rather than later.

Yankees manager Aaron Boone told reporters Wednesday that Grisham is running “up to a decent speed” in his comeback from a right hamstring strain. Considering Grisham at normal speed is slow, it’s anyone’s guess what that actually means.
If Grisham is ready to go, it will be interesting to see what Boone decides. There are numerous examples of the Yankees opting for the veteran over an inexperienced player like Jones when the games matter most.
Both players have their warts. Neither Grisham nor Jones is a good defensive center fielder. Jones looked abysmal in center, letting a ground ball go under his glove, dropping a fly ball that hit his glove and nearly trucking Heliot Ramos in right field. Meanwhile, Grisham has trouble getting to balls over his head and in the gaps because he’s slow-footed. There’s likely a higher floor of success, though, for Grisham. Even on the balls Jones has caught, there have been instances where he doesn’t look comfortable reading the play off the bat.
So the main difference will come down to offense.
Before Grisham injured his hamstring, he was not hitting. Calls for Jones to take over were already happening. To Jones’ credit, he has produced at the plate. Even after a dreadful 0-for-6 performance with five strikeouts on Wednesday, Jones has a 113 wRC+. He is always a threat to pop a home run, and that wins ballgames in October.
Grisham has one of the best eyes on the team, rarely strikes out and works at-bats. That matters when the batters behind him would likely be Ben Rice and Judge (depending on his health).
Not that my opinion holds any weight, but I’d stick with Jones in center field. The Yankees can always use Grisham, who’s one of the most clutch hitters on the team, in big spots off the bench.
Advertisement
What will/should the Yankees playoff rotation and bullpen look like? I hate to say it, but Gerrit Cole and Max Fried are not looking like aces these days. The team is winning Will Warren’s and Carlos Rodón’s starts. How are these facts likely to influence Boone’s postseason rotation decisions? … As soon as I say this, Fried pitches a gem. Jinx. — Aaron D.
The American League East race isn’t over yet, but the likeliest outcome is the Yankees will play in a wild-card series against the Boston Red Sox. That means the Yankees will only need three starting pitchers for the first round.
Cam Schlittler should start Game 1. There’s no argument otherwise. Schlittler is one of the very best starting pitchers in the sport. You want your best pitcher going in Game 1 to give yourself the best possible chance of not facing a must-win Game 2.
From there, it’ll be a toss-up between Fried and Cole. Both pitchers have concerns attached to them.
Fried has battled command issues all season, while Cole has allowed plenty of hard contact while not getting much swing-and-miss. I’d lean toward Fried over Cole.
As for the bullpen, the Yankees could have Rodón in case the club needs length. The others likely to be on the roster are Will Warren, David Bednar, Brent Headrick, Paul Blackburn, John Schreiber, Clarke Schmidt, Ryan Yarbrough and Ryan Weathers, if he’s healthy. I’d leave off Tim Hill, who has struggled mightily this season, Luis Gil and Michael Fulmer.
What is the realistic outlook for second base next year? Jazz Chisholm Jr. hasn’t played up to his talent, which might make him more enticing by bringing down his cost. The infield is already crowded, though, with Ryan McMahon under contract, George Lombard Jr.’s promotion, José Caballero, two first basemen (three if Paul Goldschmidt is still seen as Giancarlo Stanton insurance), and Anthony Volpe’s re-ascension. — Marco F.
What the Yankees decide to do at second base is one of the most fascinating storylines of the offseason.
Advertisement
I agree with you, Marco, that this season has likely cost Chisholm millions. He is nearing the end of his worst offensive season since 2021. He won’t reach the heights he set for himself entering 2026, but he still could reach a 20-40 season. Few players have the talent to post those numbers. Before this year, Chisholm posted back-to-back 4+ fWAR seasons. It would not be wrong for the Yankees or another team to bet on his upside.
Chisholm still offers tremendous defense at second and excellent baserunning. If his bat gets back to being considerably above average, he profiles as one of the best second basemen in the sport. There are valid concerns about his offense, though. His hit tool is considerably below average, and as he ages and loses athleticism, that could be a major problem that he cannot overcome.
The Yankees should consider giving Chisholm a short-term deal, though. He is a better option than Caballero and Volpe, who are better as role players, and few available players are better than what he can provide.
The Yankees should strongly consider playing Caballero or Volpe, who played a few games in the minors there, at third base. McMahon is one of the worst everyday regulars in the big leagues this season, and there’s a higher likelihood of Caballero or Volpe producing at the plate.
Has the Martian played his last game in a Yankees uniform? — oconnell13
It’s a hard question to answer because you can’t predict injuries. You never know if the Yankees will have to reach into the minor leagues for depth.
But it’s not far-fetched to think Jasson Domínguez will never play in another important game for the Yankees again. He cannot be trusted in the field. Every game matters for the Yankees, and there’s always a queasy feeling when the ball is hit his way.
His bat also hasn’t progressed enough to keep giving him chances to prove himself. Jones has leapfrogged him on the depth chart, and the Yankees now have Heliot Ramos on their roster. There may not be space for Domínguez.

What are the Yankees’ pitching plans for the rest of the regular season? Specifically, who’s lining up for the Rays series and will any of them be limited in terms of pitch count? — Nick B.
As of now, the Yankees are lined up to start their best four starters against the Rays next week. Here’s how it looks:
Tuesday: Fried and Rodón are in line to start the games of the doubleheader.
Wednesday: Cole
Thursday: Schlittler
The Rays are also on track to start their best pitchers for that series. They could start Nick Martinez and Drew Rasmussen on Tuesday, Freddy Peralta on Wednesday and Ian Seymour on Thursday. Their rotation is dependent on what they decide to do for their weekend series against the Boston Red Sox. But if they wanted, all of these pitchers could factor into their pitching plans next week.
Any chance the Yanks consider Ben Rice as the backup catcher on the postseason roster to free up an extra bench spot for someone more versatile (and better than) Ali Sánchez/J.C. Escarra? — Matthew L.
The odds of this happening are close to zero.
Earlier in the season, Rice kept catching behind the scenes. Before games, he’d catch bullpens and do on-field drills with director of catching Tanner Swanson. Rice hasn’t done any of that in months.
If anything, Rice would only be used in an emergency situation. Believe it or not, the organization believes in Sánchez. That’s why they didn’t promote Mitch Garver. Sánchez is out of minor league options, so they’d have to designate him for assignment and risk him getting claimed off waivers. They value the consistency he provides to their pitchers, and they think he’s a better defender than the metrics show.

It's been a nice start to the week in the Yankees' home-away-from-home. On Monday night, they clinched a postseason berth with a 7-3 win against the Twins. On Tuesday evening, they fielded the proverbial "hangover lineup" of sorts and still cruised to an 8-1 victory behind a strong start from Max Fried and plenty of strong performances at the plate.
On today's getaway day game in Minneapolis, Carlos Rodón leads the Yankees' effort for a sweep. His most recent start against the Mets was perhaps the best of his season, as he held down the crosstown rivals for one run in 6.1 innings—with eight strikeouts to just one walk. For Rodón, who has for various reasons not pitched deep into games as routinely as he did in 2025, a second straight start of six or more innings would be an excellent sign as he prepares for the postseason.
The Twins, now 4-9 in September, will look to young righty Zebby Matthews, who has turned in an uneven campaign on the hill this season. His past three starts have been illustrative of the step-forward-step-back tendency which has tormented many a young hurler. On August 30th, he twirled an absolute gem, pitching into the ninth inning against the rival White Sox with just one run allowed in a win. His next appearance, also against Chicago, was a far more pedestrian five-inning, four-run effort. Then last time out, he failed to escape the third inning in Detroit—walking four batters and surrendering five runs to hit the showers early.
While the Yankees rested a few of their starters for last night's contest, including Aaron Judge, it didn't prevent them from running up the score. Today, Judge returns to the lineup card, hitting third behind DH Ben Rice and Cody Bellinger, who led the way with three hits and a homer last night. Cleanup hitter Luis García Jr., Spencer Jones, and George Lombard Jr. will make up the middle of the order, with Ryan McMahon, Austin Wells, and second baseman Anthony Volpe (it's still weird to say that) pulling up the rear.

item.content:encoded:
MINNEAPOLIS — Los Yankees han resuelto la gran incógnita de septiembre. Vuelven a octubre.
Ahora, el entrenador de los Yankees, Aaron Boone, tiene otra decisión que se vuelve cada vez más urgente: ¿quién debería jugar en tercera base cuando empiece la postemporada?
Durante casi toda la temporada, Ryan McMahon parecía la respuesta más obvia. Era el tercera base titular y un defensor de probada eficacia.
Pero la plantilla de Nueva York ha cambiado a su alrededor, lo que da a los Yankees más de una opción para formar el cuadro interior, ahora que cada turno al bate y cada entrada defensiva de la postemporada tienen más importancia.
Los Yankees también cuentan con una opción más rápida y versátil para el cuadro, capaz de cubrir varias posiciones sin obligar a Boone a recurrir a una estructura de platooning demasiado limitada. Una posición que parecía decidida se ha convertido en una auténtica incógnita de cara a la postemporada.
La alineación del martes ha cambiado el debate sobre la tercera base
McMahon estaba en el banquillo de los Yankees el martes. José Caballero fue titular en tercera base una noche después de que su actuación, con dos hits y dos carreras impulsadas, ayudara a Nueva York a asegurarse el título.
Lo más revelador es que Minnesota alineó al lanzador diestro Bailey Ober. McMahon, un bateador zurdo, había vuelto a ser titular en la tercera base en la mayoría de los partidos contra lanzadores diestros tras recuperarse de un esguince de grado 2 en el pulgar izquierdo el 1 de septiembre. Por eso, la titularidad de Caballero fue algo más que una simple decisión de rotación.
No supone un cambio permanente, pero hace que la comparación sea difícil de ignorar.
Hasta el martes, Caballero ha jugado 127 partidos y tiene un promedio de bateo de .235/.292/.376, con 14 jonrones, 49 carreras impulsadas y 32 bases robadas en 429 turnos al bate. McMahon ha jugado 117 partidos y tiene un promedio de bateo de .214/.280/.353, con 10 jonrones, 34 carreras impulsadas y tres bases robadas en 340 turnos al bate.
La comparación de Stathead que se ofrece muestra a Caballero con un WAR de 2,3 frente al 0,2 de McMahon. Caballero también tiene un OPS+ de 85 frente al 75 de McMahon.
La diferencia en ataque no es enorme, pero Caballero lidera todas las categorías estadísticas mencionadas y, además, suma cuatro jonrones más, 15 carreras impulsadas más y 29 bases robadas más. En octubre, esa velocidad extra puede ser importante, incluso cuando no se espera que ninguno de los dos jugadores sea el pilar de la alineación.
Caballero no dejaba de abrirse paso en la alineación
Cuando Caballero volvió de la lista de lesionados en mayo, Boone dijo que tanto él como Anthony Volpe se habían ganado minutos de juego y que los Yankees tendrían que hacer algunos cambios para dárselos.
Boone describió la competencia como una ventaja más que como un problema.
«Es una buena situación», dijo Boone, «porque tenemos dos jugadores que creemos que pueden desempeñar un papel clave para que ganemos los partidos».
Desde entonces, la alineación ha cambiado varias veces. La lesión en el pulgar de Jazz Chisholm Jr. hizo que Caballero pasara a jugar de segunda base la semana pasada. George Lombard Jr. y Volpe se han encargado de la posición de campo corto. Caballero ha seguido jugando dondequiera que Boone lo haya necesitado.
Esa flexibilidad ha dado lugar ahora a una duda mucho mayor de cara a octubre.
McMahon aporta experiencia y un largo historial defensivo. Caballero aporta velocidad, versatilidad defensiva y la capacidad de cubrir la segunda base, el campo corto y la tercera base sin obligar a Boone a limitarse a un papel de platoon.
El caso de Caballero va más allá del guante
El historial defensivo de McMahon hace que esto no sea una simple comparación ofensiva. Baseball-Reference le atribuye 69 «Defensive Runs Saved» (DRS) a lo largo de su carrera en tercera base. Esta temporada, sin embargo, tiene un DRS de -1 en 825 1/3 entradas jugadas en esa posición.
Caballero no tiene el volumen de partidos de McMahon en esa posición, pero su historial defensivo habla por sí solo.
A lo largo de su carrera en las Grandes Ligas en las tres posiciones del cuadro, Caballero ha registrado un DRS de +10 y un Fielding Run Value de +7 en segunda base en 903 entradas, un DRS de +5 y un FRV de +4 en tercera base en 568 1/3 entradas, y un DRS de +17 con un FRV de +10 en el campo corto en 1.763 2/3 entradas.
Por eso su caso es diferente al de un suplente que se pone en racha en el momento adecuado. Los Yankees pueden poner a Caballero en tercera sin renunciar a esa versatilidad defensiva que ya lo hace útil en otras posiciones.
Su juego en las bases aumenta la ventaja. Las 32 bases robadas de Caballero le dan a Boone un arma para los momentos decisivos del partido sin que tenga que reservar a Caballero exclusivamente para entrar como corredor suplente. Si sale de titular, esa velocidad ya está en el campo.
Además, al bate, es mejor que McMahon. Hasta el 15 de septiembre, tiene un promedio de bateo de .235/.292/.376, con 14 jonrones, 49 carreras impulsadas, 32 bases robadas y un OPS de .668. McMahon se queda en un promedio de bateo de .214/.280/.353, con 10 jonrones, 34 carreras impulsadas, tres bases robadas y un OPS de .633. Caballero también tiene un WAR de 2,3, frente al 0,2 de McMahon, lo que aporta a los Yankees más producción ofensiva, velocidad y valor general sin sacrificar la flexibilidad posicional.
Ninguno de los dos ha sido un bateador por encima de la media, pero esa diferencia cuenta ahora que Boone está decidiendo su alineación para octubre. La ventaja de Caballero ya no se basa solo en su versatilidad. Simplemente ha rendido más al bate esta temporada.
Ahora hay una diferencia de 2,1 WAR que se decidirá en octubre
La diferencia más clara en general es la de 2,1 victorias en WAR.
Caballero ha sumado 2,3 WAR en 429 turnos al bate. McMahon ha sumado 0,2 en 340. A Caballero solo le han hecho falta 89 turnos al bate más para crear esa diferencia.
McMahon sigue aportando ventajas reales. Cuenta con un amplio historial defensivo en tercera base, tiene contrato hasta 2027 y puede dar un giro a la situación con un buen final de temporada. Además, hace solo dos semanas que volvió tras la lesión en el pulgar, lo que da a los Yankees motivos para tener en cuenta las dificultades recientes.
Pero los puestos en la postemporada no se otorgan en función del tipo de contrato ni de cómo se te haya utilizado antes. Nueva York ya se ha clasificado, lo que convierte el calendario que queda en una lucha por el título de división y, al mismo tiempo, en una prueba de fuego de cara a octubre.
El lunes quedó claro que Caballero puede cambiar el rumbo de un partido con su bate y sus piernas. El martes se vio que Boone está dispuesto a alinearlo directamente en la posición de McMahon, incluso contra un lanzador diestro.
Nada garantiza que esa configuración se mantenga en octubre. Los Yankees aún tienen tiempo para probarla.
Lo que sí ha cambiado es la carga de la prueba. Caballero ya no parece un jugador polivalente al que los Yankees tienen que meter a la fuerza en un partido de postemporada. Parece un jugador capaz de ganarse un puesto en la alineación titular.
Si esto sigue así, puede que sea el papel de McMahon en octubre el que tenga que reducirse.
¿Qué te parece? Deja tu comentario más abajo.

MINNEAPOLIS — When the Yankees wrapped up their spot in the postseason Monday night, Aaron Boone joined some select company.
He became the second manager in MLB history to reach the postseason in at least eight of his first nine seasons, joining Dodgers manager Dave Roberts, who has now done it in each of his first 11 seasons. Boone is also the third manager to make the playoffs in eight of his first nine seasons with the Yankees, joining Joe Torre and Casey Stengel.

Join Post Sports+ for exciting subscriber-only features, including real-time texting with Greg Joyce about the inside buzz on the Yankees.
Try it free
Of course, Roberts, Torre and Stengel have combined to win 14 World Series titles while Boone is still in search of his first. And ultimately, in New York, that is how he will be judged, as opposed to just getting his team to the postseason regularly.
But in a season in which the Yankees have had most of their biggest stars spend sizable chunks of time on the injured list, Boone has helped lead them through the adversity to still have as good a chance as any team in the American League to make a run to the World Series.
“He’s our guy,” Aaron Judge said in the champagne-soaked visitors clubhouse at Target Field late Monday night. “He’s the one we go to battle for every single night and just lucky and blessed to have him here, to be able to fight for a guy like that. He loves every single guy in this room and we’re going to fight till the end for him.”
The Yankees still have bigger things left to accomplish this year, starting with trying to chase down the Rays for the division, but then more importantly, attempting to go the distance in October for the first time since 2009.
But by the time they clinched their playoff spot, the Yankees had survived 84 games without Judge; 124 games and counting without Giancarlo Stanton; 25 games without Cody Bellinger; 27 games and counting without Trent Grisham (across two IL stints); 22 games without Ryan McMahon (across two IL stints); 51 games without Gerrit Cole; 71 games without Max Fried (across two IL stints); 40 games without Carlos Rodón (across two IL stints); 21 games and counting without Ryan Weathers; and 150 games and counting without Clarke Schmidt, among others.
Every team deals with injuries, but not every team survives them to the extent that the Yankees have, entering Tuesday on pace to match the 94 wins they have had in each of the last two seasons.
“It’s very tough for a Yankee manager to win Manager of the Year,” bench coach Brad Ausmus said Tuesday, pointing to the high expectations with which the franchise enters every season. “Obviously [Rays manager] Kevin Cash and [White Sox manager] Will Venable will be extremely strong candidates. But with the job [Boone] has done this year with the injuries, keeping the group as one cohesive unit, I think he should definitely be in the discussion.”
There were some rough stretches along the way during Judge’s three-month absence, most notably a 5-15 skid from late June to early July.
Shop Yankees Merch
Even when the Yankees started to snap out of that, it did not often feel like it as their offense was still in a malaise and almost every game they played was a low-scoring, nail-biting battle.
Though that stretch threatens to ultimately cost the Yankees a chance at overtaking the Rays for the AL East, Boone is hoping he will have his team in a position to be at its best in the postseason to make a run at an elusive title.
“It’s not easy,” Austin Wells said. “You lose guys left and right at different parts of the season. Having to piece wins together, keep us right there in the division race throughout the whole year, he does an impressive job. Definitely a testament to him. Looking forward to more of that, more winning decisions and keep leading us.”

item.content:encoded:
MINNEAPOLIS — Durante siete entradas, la ofensiva de los Yankees apenas hizo nada contra Minnesota, mientras que los errores defensivos complicaron una noche en la que ya había mucho en juego de cara a octubre.
Pero la octava entrada lo cambió todo.
George Lombard Jr. abrió el partido con un doble, Ryan McMahon llegó a base y José Caballero empató el partido con un sencillo. Anthony Volpe y Caballero encadenaron un doble robo antes de que Ben Rice conectara un sencillo de dos carreras al centro. De repente, los Yankees se pusieron por delante 4-2.
Aaron Judge asestó el golpe definitivo. Después de que Cody Bellinger llegara a base, Judge mandó un cutter de A.J. Minter a las gradas del campo izquierdo para un jonrón de tres carreras, el primero para él desde el 24 de mayo. Austin Wells añadió un jonrón solitario en la novena entrada, y los Yankees cerraron la victoria por 8-3, lo que les aseguró su 61.ª clasificación para la postemporada y la novena en las últimas diez temporadas.
Según el marcador oficial, la victoria fue para Tim Hill, la derrota para Andrew Morris y John Schreiber sumó su segundo salvamento. Will Warren encajó dos carreras no ganadas en 5 2/3 entradas. Tras el partido, los Yankees quedan con un balance de 87-63, a 3,5 partidos de los Tampa Bay Rays, líderes de la División Este de la Liga Americana.
Ben Rice acabó con 2 de 3, dos carreras impulsadas y una base por bolas. Judge por fin se desató después de llegar al partido con un registro de 3 de 20 y 11 strikeouts desde que volvió tras una ausencia de 84 partidos por una fractura en la costilla derecha.
La primera carrera de los Yankees llegó con el jonrón de Caballero en la tercera entrada, pero Minnesota se puso por delante en la sexta después de que un error de Ryan McMahon ayudara a alargar la entrada y Emmanuel Rodríguez impulsara dos carreras con un triple. Los Yankees solo habían conseguido dos hits en siete entradas. La victoria de Detroit por 6-5 sobre Toronto aseguró matemáticamente la clasificación de Nueva York para la postemporada durante el partido, pero los Yankees aún así remataron la faena con su 35.ª remontada de la temporada.
Ese contexto fue importante el lunes por la noche.
Pero lo más raro ocurrió después de que los Yankees se pusieran por delante, cuando la retransmisión televisiva de Minnesota pasó de mostrar el jonrón de Judge a enfocar los movimientos de Rice en la segunda base.
La cabina de los Twins pone a Rice bajo la lupa
La retransmisión de Twins.TV volvió a mostrar a Rice durante el turno al bate de Judge y comparó su lenguaje corporal ante los distintos lanzamientos de Minter. Rice pareció hacer un movimiento evidente antes de un cambio de velocidad, pero no lo repitió antes del cutter que Judge conectó para el jonrón de tres carreras.
Eso llevó a los comentaristas a preguntarse si Rice había captado algo de Minter y le estaba pasando información sobre los lanzamientos a Judge.
La retransmisión también reconoció la diferencia clave: no presentó ninguna prueba de que los Yankees utilizaran dispositivos electrónicos, vídeo o cualquier otro sistema prohibido.
Un comentarista de los Twins dijo mientras se mostraba la repetición:
«Solo estamos contando lo que vimos. Por la derecha lanzaba un cambio de velocidad, por la izquierda una bola rápida. Por la derecha nunca se agacha hasta las rodillas. Entonces, ¿había algo ahí? Solo ellos lo saben, pero todo dentro de las reglas del juego».
El equipo de Twins.TV del lunes estaba formado por Corey Provus, Justin Morneau, Trevor Plouffe y Audra Martin. La transcripción disponible no permite identificar con certeza a quién pertenecía la voz que hizo el comentario, así que en este artículo no se atribuye a ningún comentarista en concreto.
Esa última frase es importante. La MLB distingue entre la observación en el campo y el uso prohibido de dispositivos electrónicos o de vídeo para descifrar las señales. Las restricciones sobre el robo de señales mediante dispositivos electrónicos se aclararon y reforzaron en 2017 y 2018. Nada de lo que se mostró el lunes demostró que los Yankees hubieran cruzado esa línea.
El juez hace que cuente cada lanzamiento
La sospecha llamó la atención por lo que pasó después.
Judge había parecido un poco fuera de forma durante gran parte de su primera semana tras el regreso. Había hecho un roletazo que se convirtió en doble play y se había ponchado dos veces antes de que Minter lanzara un cutter por dentro que Judge mandó fuera. Ese jonrón fue el decimoctavo de Judge en la temporada y convirtió una ventaja de dos carreras en un colchón de cinco.
La reacción de Rice dejó claro lo rápido que ese turno al bate cambió el rumbo de la noche.
«¡Madre mía, menuda jugada!», dijo Rice. «Menudo golpe. Uno se podría acostumbrar a ver algo así, sobre todo en esta época del año».
El repunte de Rice en septiembre le da un nuevo matiz
Las estadísticas actualizadas de la temporada hasta el 14 de septiembre muestran que Rice tiene un promedio de bateo de .263, con 38 jonrones, 92 carreras impulsadas, 96 carreras anotadas y un OPS de .888 en 143 partidos.
Un análisis de PinstripesNation de esos resultados partido a partido muestra una racha reciente aún más impresionante. En nueve partidos desde el 4 de septiembre, Rice ha conectado 13 de 31, un promedio de .419, con tres jonrones, cinco carreras impulsadas y siete bases por bolas.
Esa aportación fue clave durante la larga ausencia de Judge. El sencillo de dos carreras de Rice el lunes dio a los Yankees su primera ventaja después de que Minnesota se pusiera 2-1 por delante en la sexta entrada.
No hay pruebas de que los Yankees hayan urdido un plan ilegal
La repetición de la retransmisión creó un momento polémico, pero las pruebas disponibles distan mucho de demostrar que se haya producido un robo ilegal de señales.
No ha habido ningún indicio público de que la MLB esté investigando a Rice, a Judge o a los Yankees por esa jugada. Tampoco hay pruebas de que se utilizara tecnología para descifrar los lanzamientos de Minter.
Aún no se ha aclarado públicamente si los movimientos de Rice fueron señales intencionadas o simplemente el comportamiento habitual de un corredor de bases.
Los Yankees ganaron porque su octava entrada desbordó al bullpen de Minnesota. Caballero empató el partido, Rice conectó el hit que les dio la ventaja y Judge aprovechó un cutter para sumar tres carreras más. Schreiber cerró luego la victoria por 8-3 con una doble jugada que puso fin al partido.
Para los Yankees, el resultado general está asegurado. Vuelven a octubre. No hay nada que se haya hecho público que demuestre que Rice o los Yankees hayan infringido las normas de la MLB.
¿Qué opinas? Deja tu comentario más abajo.

But a few names are missing from that list: Shortstop George Lombard Jr., outfielder Spencer Jones, first baseman Luis García Jr. and outfielder Heliot Ramos. Those four have never played in the postseason, either with the Yankees or -- as is the case with García and Ramos -- with their previous teams.
Now, it’s possible that some of the injured veteran players -- Grisham and Chisholm, specifically -- could return to the lineup and send some of those new faces to the bench or off the playoff roster entirely. But it’s safe to say the Yankees are going to be counting on at least a few playoff newbies next month in their quest to win their first World Series since 2009.
Yankees manager Aaron Boone said his youngsters and playoff newcomers have another advantage over players who are coming of age in other markets.
“You play for the Yankees, you play in New York,” he said, “it has a way of getting you ready for the postseason.”
This has been something of a transitional year in the Major Leagues. Check out the first round of the 2023 Draft if you want proof. No fewer than 19 of the 37 first-round and sandwich picks have debuted, and many of them are already impact players with their teams.
“Players are getting to the big leagues at a very quick pace now and at a young age,” said Tigers manager A.J. Hinch, who has welcomed No. 3 pick Max Clark and AL Rookie of the Year favorite Kevin McGonigle to Detroit this year. “I don't think they're as wowed by the big steps that they're taking.”
For the Yankees, that class includes Lombard, who has acclimated nicely since being called up in early August. And Jones was recently lauded by none other than Aaron Judge, who said the rookie outfielder has “really evolved every single time he got called up, gotten a little bit better and a little bit better.”
Of course, there will be hiccups along the way. On Wednesday, Jones went 0-for-6 with five strikeouts and committed an error when he dropped a fly ball in center field. And Lombard couldn’t come up with a Victor Caratini grounder in the 13th that was ruled a single as the Twins walked off the Yankees.
But anyone who follows baseball knows bad days and bad plays are all part of the growth cycle of a Major League player. The key is to learn from them so you can limit them going forward. And all of it -- the good, the bad and the occasionally ugly -- helps prepare a young player for his first time playing in the crucible of October baseball.
The world is about to find out just how ready the young Yankees are. But Jones offered a bit of reassurance on Monday as he soaked up the post-clinch locker room celebration at Target Field.
“I think for us, we play better when the crowd gets louder,” he said. “I’m really excited for what’s to come.”

Will the New York Yankees replace Ryan McMahon at third base this offseason?
The results have not been what Yankees fans were expecting.
Since arriving in the Bronx in July 2025, McMahon is slashing just .211/.290/.346 with 14 home runs and 52 RBI over 522 plate appearances.
This season, he owns a .212/.280/.353 slash line with 10 homers and 34 RBI across 337 trips to the dish, and while McMahon does seem to have an odd knack for getting big hits, his offensive production has been generally unacceptable at the hot corner.
New York was willing to look past that because of his defense, as McMahon posted 10 defensive runs saved and seven outs above average at third base last year. He also regularly posted similar numbers during his time with the Colorado Rockies.
While McMahon has still been wholly solid in the field, a 2026 decline has been evident, as he has posted zero defensive runs saved and three outs above average this season.
Has he been bad at third? Absolutely not. But he has been good enough to justify his $16 million salary while posting a .633 OPS? No.
The problem for the Yankees is that McMahon is under contract for another $16 million next year, which significantly decreases the chances of New York going out and finding an upgrade at the position.
These aren't your dad's Yankees; this is the more financially shrewd, cost-conscious version that initially balked at making any major moves last year due to Marcus Stroman's $18 million salary ... which they eventually ate after releasing him in August 2025.
You can bet that Hal Steinbrenner has every intention of going into 2027 with McMahon as the club's starting third baseman unless Brian Cashman can somehow find a trade for the veteran in which he can offload that money.
McMahon is 31 years old. He'll turn 32 in December. It's entirely possible that the former All-Star is declining, so it's possible that his defensive downturn this season is not a mirage.
Can New York win with McMahon on the roster? Sure. But is it preferable to keep him in a starting role? No.
An alternative solution is fighting a right-handed third baseman who isn't Amed Rosario to man the starting job while keeping McMahon in a reserve role ... but then you are paying $16 million for a pedestrian bench player. That isn't exactly advisable. Especially not for a team that, in recent years, has been trying to cut costs.
And it becomes even less realistic if the MLB does, indeed, institute a salary cap for 2027.
Is it possible the Yankees can trade McMahon? I guess, but good luck finding a team willing to take on the final year of his contract. New York would likely have to absorb some of that $16 million salary, and I'm just not sure how amenable Steinbrenner would be to doing that.
You would think if it meant upgrading the team for just a little bit of extra case, the Yankees would do it. I mean, they're the Yankees, right? But those Evil Empire days appear to be long gone.
The most probable scenario is New York opening up 2027 with McMahon as its starting third baseman, and while it could be worse, it could also be a lot better.

José Caballero has not been in the starting lineup for each of the first two games.
UPDATE: The Yankees won 2-0 on Sunday.
Caballero had one walk and two strikeouts.
Yankees Announce Caballero Decision
For Sunday’s game, the Yankees have announced their starting lineup.
Via FantasyPros: “NYY Yankees Lineup 09/13 1. Ben Rice DH 2. Cody Bellinger LF 3. Aaron Judge RF 4. Luis Garcia 1B 5. Spencer Jones CF 6. Anthony Volpe 2B 7. Ryan McMahon 3B 8. Austin Wells C 9. Jose Caballero SS”
Caballero is back in the lineup.
He is starting at shortstop (and hitting 9th).
Right now, the 30-year-old is batting .233 with 89 hits, 13 home runs, 47 RBIs, 46 runs and 31 stolen bases in 125 games.
Caballero has been a solid addition to the Yankees since joining the franchise last season.
Over four total seasons at the MLB level, he has also had stops with the Seattle Mariners and Tampa Bay Rays.
In 2025, Caballero stole 49 bases.
Looking At The Yankees Right Now
The Yankees are the second-place team in the American League East with an 85-63 record in 148 games.
They have won seven out of their last ten games (and are 41-32 in 73 games at home in the Bronx).
Looking At The Mets Right Now
The Mets are the fourth-place team in the National League East with a 69-79 record in 148 games.
They have won seven out of their last ten games (and are 35-39 in 74 games on the road away from Citi Field).
